Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs. They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence. Canada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too. For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships. But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership. Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries. No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example. A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU. Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc. In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side.

item.title: Google's Gemini AI hacked three companies in security test
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.70
- Published Google's AI model Gemini autonomously hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security capabilities, the company has said, in what is thought to be the first known case of it carrying out such an act. Gemini found "public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test", a Google official told the BBC, noting that in each instance "the model stopped". The affected companies have been informed about the breach. It comes after renewed public scrutiny over the pace of AI development, with some tech firms calling for a slowdown as they raise concerns over its potential threat to humanity - though not all companies agree. The hacks first reported by the Wall Street Journal, occurred in May during a test conducted by an independent company that carries out cyber-security evaluations. Heather Adkins, vice president of Security Engineering at Google, told the BBC in a statement: "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes." She added: "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly." Other AI systems have recently reported similar instances of breaches. In July, Anthropic's Claude escaped its test environment to hack three organisations on its own just days after OpenAI said its models had carried out cyber-attacks against several "publicly available services". As public debate continues to grow over the safety of developing the tech, so too does conversation around regulation. Both Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman are expected to attend a White House state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping next Friday. Altman will then brief the UN Security Council next week. On Friday, Huang told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, "we should go as fast as we can" with AI development.

item.title: Aztec document goes on display in Mexico after 186 years abroad
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.61
- Published A centuries-old document telling the story of the Aztec civilisation and its fall after the arrival of the Spanish conquistadors in pictograms is going on display in Mexico for the first time in 186 years. The manuscript, known as Codex Azcatitlán, has been held in France's Bibliothèque Nationale since 1898, but had already spent decades outside of Mexico before that. It is thought to have been drawn in the 16th Century - a few years after the arrival of the conquistadors in what is now Mexico - and is widely considered one of the most valuable and insightful tellings of the history of the Aztecs. France has lent Codex Azcatitlán to Mexico to mark 200 years of Franco-Mexican relations. In return, Mexico has agreed to lend another priceless document, the Codex Boturini, to France for display there. The pictograms in the Codex Boturini narrate the story of the migration of the Aztecs, also known as Mexica, from their ancestral homeland to the shores of Lake Texcoco, where they built Tenochtitlán. The temporary exchange of the two codices was agreed by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and her French counterpart, Emmanuel Macron, during a visit by the latter to Mexico last year. Mexico has long lobbied for the return of historical artefacts taken from the country in past centuries. According to Mexico's ministry of foreign relations, last year more than 2,000 objects were successfully repatriated. The Codex Azcatitlán will be exhibited at the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City from Thursday.

item.title: Verified video shows wreckage of Saudi fighter jet shot down over Yemen
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.44
- Published Footage verified by the BBC shows the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet which the Iran-backed Houthi group says it shot down over Yemen. The US-made aircraft was "downed using a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile" as it "conducted hostile operations" over the Marib region, according to a Houthi statement on Wednesday. Experts have told BBC Verify the incident is a "propaganda coup" that shows the Houthis' military capability has advanced and they are prepared to further escalate its conflict with Saudi Arabia. Using satellite imagery to match features in the landscape seen in the footage, BBC Verify was able to pinpoint the crash site to an isolated location in the hills west of the Yemeni city of Marib. The long-running conflict between a Saudi-led military coalition and the Houthis has escalated in the last week after the armed group launched an offensive against pro-government forces. This led to the Houthis seizing key territory near the south-west coast, close to vital international shipping channels in the Bab al-Mandab strait. In one of several video clips released by the Houthis, men with assault rifles can be seen at the crash site inspecting the wreckage. The fighters celebrate as they lift the jet's almost-intact tail fin which features the Saudi flag and a four-digit serial number. The fate of of the crew is not known. The Houthis also released a thermal video clip - which cannot be fully verified due to a lack of visual details - that appears to show a fighter jet in mid-flight being struck by a missile. BBC Verify has contacted the Saudi Ministry of Defence for comment. Baraa Shiban, Yemen analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told BBC Verify the incident showed it was "very clear the Houthis have been taking advantage of advice and technological support" from Iran. "They continue to develop their military arsenal and capabilities to make it more and more painful on Saudi Arabia," he said. Downing the F-15 is also a "propaganda coup", said Yemen expert Adam Baron from the Washington-based New America think tank, as Saudi air support is considered to be "key to any significant pushback" against recent Houthi gains. "An eye-for-an-eye has been a huge element of the group's public messaging. This is partially to show that air support will come at a price," he added. BBC Verify used the position of the sun and satellite imagery to locate the distinctive landscape seen in the footage - including cliff faces and hills - to an isolated mountainous area about 25 miles (40km) west of Marib. Satellite imagery published on Wednesday also shows a new dark shadow at the same location, which appears consistent with scorch or burn marks at a crash site. The aircraft in the wreckage has been independently identified by Nick Brown, a weapons expert from military intelligence company Janes, as an F-15 Strike Eagle. He based his analysis on distinctive elements seen in the footage including the tail fin arrangement, radar antenna and missile warning system sensors. The four-digit tail number visible on the wreckage also appears to be consistent with that of an F-15 Strike Eagle operated by the 55th Squadron of the Royal Saudi Air Force based at King Khalid Air Base near the city of Khamis Mushait in south-west Saudi Arabia. This base, about 245 miles (392 km) from the crash site, was targeted last week by what the Houthis described as a "barrage of missiles and drones". Satellite imagery analysed by BBC Verify appears to show damage to at least three aircraft hangars or shelters. The base is one of a series of high-profile Saudi targets struck by the Houthis in recent days including an oil refinery in the city of Jizan. Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday it had destroyed a Houthi drone close to the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, which the Houthis have denied targeting. The group said on Thursday that Saudi Arabia had launched 40 air strikes against Yemen over the past 24 hours. Additional reporting by Shayan Sardarizadeh and Alex Murray Graphics by Tom Shiel

item.title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.26
- Published Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way. His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb. But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta. And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present. "If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can." Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society. As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together. That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs. The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries. Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply. We don't have food. We don't have medicine. People will struggle. If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated." There are many risks. If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator. But if they call ahead, information could leak. "Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said. "Absolutely. Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming." By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism. "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us. You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver." Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters. "It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said. "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians. Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta. We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines. She lost her home and her husband during the full-scale invasion, and came to the area to rebuild her life. She ran the post office in the village of Lukasheve for two years until it was destroyed in March by a Russian drone, targeting soldiers working nearby. After her van drew up, a steady queue of elderly folk formed. She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments. One customer, Nadiia, said she was grateful: "It's a long way for us to travel to Zaporizhzhia. Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us. The fact that they come here is really nice." Oleksandrivna, 77, arrived wearing a purple dressing gown, walking with a crutch. When I asked her where she would be without Kateryna, she replied: "We would be stuffed! I am just out of hospital after a stroke. Where could I go for my medicine?" But Mykola, 64, pointed to another service the post office provides to a largely elderly population. "It is very important," he said. "It's one of the few joys of the month: you come out, have a chat with people, collect your pension, and go home." For many people in remote communities, Kateryna can be their last link with the Ukrainian state. She says she hopes her customers are proud of her. "They love me, they need me," she said. "They are waiting for me. Sometimes they call me, especially after attacks on Zaporizhzhia and ask me how I am. We are like a big family. My attitude towards them is like a grandmother or grandfather." The attacks on Ukrposhta form part of Russia's wider escalation of its war on Ukraine, stepping up fast drone attacks on civilian infrastructure including business infrastructure, energy facilities, transport networks and border posts. Analysts say that as Russia's invasion stagnates on the battlefield in the east, it is looking for other ways of putting pressure on Kyiv. For safety, Kateryna always travels with her partner, Slava, who drives. While she sorts the cash, he works from the back of the van, taking and receiving parcels, delivering food and water. He also carries a side-arm in a holster, for personal protection; these vans carry a lot of cash. Both wear body armour when close to the front line. And they have an antenna in the van that shows them the location of the small first-person-view drones that render the frontline so deadly. They have seen drones from the car but luckily have not yet been hit. She accepted her job was dangerous but would never change it. "It is my work," she said. "If I can't, who will do my job?" Ukraine's defence comes in many forms - and it's not always delivered at the barrel of a gun. Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk

item.title: Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.24
- Published French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France has intensified. In a news conference at the Elysee Palace, Macron said he had ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites in the face of this threat. He said France had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks which would not be left "without a response". A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine. Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank. "In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said. "The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine." On Thursday Tusk told Polish MPs that Russian plans included strikes by drones and missiles on countries supporting Ukraine. He said there was a "real risk" of such strikes on the territory of Nato countries, with Moscow then claiming that they were "accidental", in an attempt to split the alliance. Last Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line. Ukraine said all the passengers had been evacuated just minutes before the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Russia does not plan to attack Europe, but Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned European nations against sending troops to Ukraine, which would be seen by Russia as a declaration of war. "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short," he said. Meanwhile on Friday, Russia reiterated its warning to the UK that any British military facilities in Ukraine used to strike Russian territory were "legitimate targets". It reserved the right to take "necessary counter-measures" in response to the UK's "fiercely confrontational stance regarding Ukraine", referring to its supply of drones and other weapon systems to Kyiv. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Macron also addressed the energy situation, saying that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks. He announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission. "In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said. "It will also be an opportunity to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves." In a domestic context, he called on candidates in next year's elections not to exploit public unease by blaming the government, but to acknowledge that fuel price inflation was the result of uncontrollable international circumstances. The hard-right opposition National Rally candidate Marine le Pen is currently leading the polls for the April-May vote to replace Macron.

item.title: International students, 'visa hoppers' and backpackers targeted in Australia migration crackdown
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.12
- Published International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to curb immigration. Foreign students will no longer be able to bring their families with them and those who want to extend their stay must choose a higher qualification. Rules will also be stricter for working holiday visas - commonly used by backpackers and a crucial labour source for the agricultural sector - with a ballot system although these changes will not affect the UK. The new rules were revealed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke who said that while immigration was a "strength" of Australia, there needed to be a "high level of control". For international student and graduate visas, Burke said: "We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over." There would be exemptions for foreign students already in Australia as well as applicants from the Pacific and South East Asian countries, he said. PhD students would also be able to bring their families as they were in different life circumstances to undergraduates, Burke said. In a speech titled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Burke revealed a raft of changes as the government aims to bring net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028. On student visas, he said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" - where a student finishes a course, then applies to do another course which is often a lower qualification and sometimes with a "not so legitimate provider". Students who want to go "up the scale" will be allowed, Burke said, for example, if a student finishes a bachelor's degree and then wants to complete a masters. He also announced major changes to working holiday visas for those aged 18 to 30 years old who can work in Australia for 12 months, but can extend for a second and third year. Currently, these visa holders must work for three months in regional Australia during their first year to qualify for a second year, and then six months to qualify for a third year. Under the new changes, those who qualify for a second year will have to go into a ballot with a cap of 45,000, down from the 57,000 who qualified last year. For the third year, the ballot will be limited to 5,000, down from 31,000 who qualified last year. British working holidaymakers will not be affected by these changes due to the UK's free trade agreement with Australia. New figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed Australia's population grew 1.4% in the 12 months to March 2026 to 27.9m. That total figure included births and deaths as well as a net overseas migration of 292,100. Migration remains a major political issue as debate around Australia's population grows amid rising living costs, housing affordability and increased strain on public services. One Nation, a populist right-wing party known for its anti-immigration stance and which has seen a surge in support in recent months, detailed its migration policy earlier this week, proposing to cut temporary migrant visas by 750,000 over three years. The party, which won its first lower house seat in May, also wants to cap net overseas immigration to 130,000, drawing a rebuke from Burke who said such a proposal would risk "smashing parts of the Australian economy". In July, the government introduced a policy to prioritise applications for family visas lodged onshore - where the applicant is in the country already - over those submitted overseas. Skilled migrants already in Australia who applied for permanent visas were also prioritised over those applying from overseas. It also paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries, not including the UK. Violet Roumeliotis, from Settlement Services International which helps new arrivals to Australia, says the migration debate was increasingly driven by "short-term politics rather than what is best for the country". "The proposed changes to family visas for international students is a good example of this," she said, adding that it would make it harder for Australia to compete for "future talent".

item.title: One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.06
- Published North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region. Spain's national weather agency AEMET issued warnings for heavy rain across eastern regions on Wednesday, including a red alert for Barcelona's coastline. Rescuers recovered the body of a man on Thursday in Olivella, around 40km (25 miles) west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away by a stream, authorities said. The deluge has disrupted travel across Catalonia and Valencia, with flights cancelled and roads submerged. Authorities have advised against unnecessary travel, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned of "very complicated situations". Emergency services in Catalonia said they received more than 850 calls related to the downpours and catalogued over 500 incidents. Catalan firefighters said on X on Thursday that they had recovered the "lifeless body of a man" in Olivella, correcting earlier reports that had identified the missing person as a woman. Videos shared on social media showed partially submerged cars and rescue workers attempting to reach a vehicle trapped in a heavily flooded underpass. In Barcelona, some metro stations were closed and buses diverted, while regional trains were disrupted and flights delayed or cancelled at El Prat airport. Neighbouring Valencia had more than 70mm (2.76in) of rain fall in just half an hour in several municipalities, according to AVAMET. "Rarely have we seen such rainfall accumulations in 30 minutes," the meteorological association said on X. Emergency services reported 478 incidents in the Valencia province, mostly involving property damage, leaks and traffic disruption. In the regional capital, all metro lines were suspended and the city's airport shuttered for several hours, causing flights to be diverted. The downpour comes as Spain emerges from its hottest summer on record and an exceptionally warm start to September. Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the Mediterranean storms that typically hit eastern Spain in autumn. The Mediterranean Sea absorbs heat during summer, increasing evaporation and contributing to heavier rainfall when storms develop. The flooding comes less than two years after devastating flooding in Valencia killed more than 230 people.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror says he had no doubt she deliberately killed her children
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.69
- Published The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating. Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated. Warning: This article contains distressing details The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window. To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition. The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder. Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible. Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings. "I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented." Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind. "We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said. The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster". She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity." Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side". But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial. The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations. Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday. In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began. He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them". During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis. Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong. A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children. However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association. Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility. The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial. Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial. He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy. He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset." The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

item.title: India faces 100% tariff threat over Russian oil after US House vote
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.68
- Published For four years, India, one of the world's biggest oil importers, has turned Russia's war-driven disruption of global oil markets to its advantage. Russian crude, displaced from western markets after the invasion of Ukraine, has flowed instead to Indian refineries, often at attractive discounts. The arrangement has lowered the cost of one of India's biggest imports and given its refiners an abundant source of crude. Now that bargain is becoming a source of geopolitical risk. The US House of Representatives on Wednesday passed legislation giving President Donald Trump broad powers to impose sanctions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100% on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. It will now go to Trump to be signed into law. India and China are among those most exposed because both are major buyers of Russian oil. China accounted for half of Russia's crude exports, followed by India at 37%, Turkey at 5% and the EU at 5% between December 2022 and August 2026, according to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). Russia supplied 30.3% of India's crude imports in fiscal 2026, worth $40.8bn out of a total crude import bill of $134.7bn, according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), a Delhi-based think tank. In July, Russian crude accounted for more than half of India's imports. Other suppliers lagged far behind: the UAE accounted for 10.8% of India's July imports, Saudi Arabia 9.6%, Venezuela 6.3%, Brazil 5.5%, Oman 5.3% and the US 2.9%. Russia alone supplied more crude than all six combined. "The bill is a blunt and dangerous attempt to pressurise India to sign the bilateral trade agreement on one-sided terms. India buys Russian oil to secure affordable energy for 1.4 billion people, not to finance war, and these purchases have helped stabilise global supplies and prices," says Ajay Srivastava, a former Indian trade official who runs GTRI. To be true, the economics of Russian oil have shifted. The crude no longer carries the steep discounts that made it particularly attractive to Indian refiners in the early years of the war, while competition for Russian barrels has intensified and shipping, insurance and sanctions risks have risen. "China and India, you better buy your oil and gas somewhere else," Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal told reporters , externalafter the passage of the bill. These countries would normally have 180 days to cut Russian energy imports or negotiate with Washington, but the president can shorten the deadline. India said in a statement that it was "monitoring further developments on this matter" and that it remained "firmly committed to ensuring energy security" for its people. "This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side," it added. India can find alternatives to Russian crude, but replacing it at scale would come at a price. S&P Global says alternative supplies, external can mean higher crude, freight and insurance costs, while longer shipping routes add to the burden. "The issue is not simply whether Russian barrels can be redirected to other buyers, but whether enough alternative crude is available to replace them without tightening the global market further," says Sumit Ritolia, an analyst at maritime intelligence firm Kpler. But the tariff would hit India elsewhere, too. The US is threatening tariffs on Indian exports to America, not a tax on Russian crude entering India. The impact would be felt through Indian exporters, the rupee, refinery margins and the trade balance. "This new bill could have major problematic impacts for India, and at the worst possible time, amid sensitive final-stage trade talks and shaky broader relations," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. "India has built some insulation to fend off the shocks of US tariffs through new trade deals with key markets in the EU and elsewhere, and through bolstering an already strong trade partnership with China. But [up to]100% tariffs from a critical export destination is real bad news, no matter how you slice it and even with successful hedging tactics." The scale of that exposure is considerable. The US imported about $104bn of goods from India in 2025, while two-way US-India trade in goods and services was roughly $240bn, according to the US Trade Representative. India's exports to the US include electronics, pharmaceuticals, machinery, jewellery, chemicals, textiles and petroleum products. In 2025, electrical and electronic equipment alone accounted for about $25.8bn of Indian exports to America, pharmaceuticals about $9.7bn and machinery about $7.2bn. The new threat comes after an earlier round of Trump tariffs on Indian goods, which peaked at 50% in 2025 before being reduced. That creates an uncomfortable calculation for Delhi: how much should India pay for Russian crude before the savings are outweighed by the risk to its exports to the US? There is no simple answer. It will depend on the Russian discount, global crude prices, freight and insurance costs, the tariff Trump ultimately imposes, and whether Washington offers exemptions or reaches a broader settlement with Delhi. The picture gets more complicated once the crude is refined. India is not merely a buyer: its refineries turn Russian crude into fuels that can then be exported. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have forced the world's once-largest oil-products exporter to import fuel. In August, imports hit a record 172,000 tonnes, more than seven times the previous monthly high, according to CREA. India supplied about 120,000 tonnes, or roughly 70%, mostly petrol refined from Russian crude at a refinery in Gujarat, worth around €78m. China buys more Russian crude than India, but Kugelman says Beijing has greater leverage because of its role in global supply chains and the scale of its economic relationship with the US. "China has massive leverage over the global economy, particularly through its dominance of critical supply chains. India, despite being one of the world's biggest economies, does not have the same leverage. The Trump administration appears to believe that its economic interests are more exposed if China retaliates than if India does," says Kugelman. For India, the issue is not simply how much Russian oil it buys, but how resilient its alternatives are. The threat is serious because India imports more than 88% of its crude oil. More than 85% of India's crude comes from just six countries, several in conflict-prone regions, while its refineries are not always equipped to switch easily between crude grades, according to the think-tank Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW). The vulnerability extends beyond oil. India imports more than 60% of its LPG, the main cooking fuel for more than 330 million households. Its strategic petroleum reserves hold only 9-10 days of net oil imports, compared with roughly 200 days in Japan and 207 in South Korea. Operational stocks at refineries provide another 64 days. All this makes Russian crude more than a bargain: CEEW estimates that India has saved about $12.6bn from its post-2022 shift to Russian crude. The looming US tariff could now turn that insurance into a liability - leaving Delhi to calculate whether the savings from Russian oil are worth the price of keeping it. GTRI's Srivastava reckons "Washington could threaten tariffs of up to 100%, then offer a lower rate if Delhi cuts Russian oil purchases and accepts concessions in a deeply unequal trade deal". "India should not allow US tariff threats to determine its energy policy," he says. "It should continue buying Russian oil as long as it remains commercially competitive and negotiate firmly with Washington without granting unilateral trade concessions."

item.title: North Korean anthem played for South Korea at Asian Games
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.30
- Published Organisers have apologised for playing the North Korean national anthem for the South Korean men's hockey team at the Asian Games in Japan. South Korea, who thrashed Bangladesh 5-0, looked confused as the incorrect national anthem was played. South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported that Bangladesh's national anthem followed before South Korea's actual anthem was played. A stadium announcer did apologise for the mistake. "This is a really serious problem. When we protested, they said, 'We're sorry. It wasn't that it wasn't prepared; there was a mistake on the part of those responsible for playing it'," South Korea coach Min Tae-seok said. "But this is something that simply should never happen." North Korea's national anthem, along with other symbols of the secretive state, are banned in South Korea. The two countries are still technically at war, after the 1950-53 conflict between the two ended without a peace treaty. The build-up to the Asian Games, which officially starts on Saturday, has already seen complaints from teams about the quality and amount of accommodation. A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me." Some teams were also stranded at the airport for up to six hours when they landed this week. Field hockey at the Asian Games started on Friday and runs until 3 October.

item.title: River home to 500 crocodiles chosen as Olympic rowing venue
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.19
- Published A river that is home to about 500 saltwater crocodiles has been given the OK to host Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing events at the 2032 Brisbane Games. The course on the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton, Queensland, has passed an independent technical assessment into its suitability. The assessment did not consider the crocodiles but instead looked at "how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the Games". The report was commissioned by the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA), which noted, external that the Fitzroy River Flatwater Facility "is already a training and competition venue for flatwater sports, supporting school state championships, local regattas, and national team training camps". As a recognised rowing facility, contingency plans are in place at events for when crocodiles are spotted and Olympic officials have previously been assured of rower safety. World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide, formerly International Canoe Federation, both endorsed the course. "Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic Rowing," World Rowing President Jean-Christophe Rolland said., external Paddle Worldwide President Thomas Konietzko said: "The quality and depth of the technical work undertaken has significantly improved our understanding of the field of play and provides confidence to us and our athletes that the course can deliver fair competition for Canoe Sprint athletes." Brisbane 2032 President Andrew Liveris played down the issue of crocodiles last year. "There are sharks in the ocean and we're still surfing... it's a can do, not a can't do - please change the mindset here," he said at the time. Speaking on Thursday about the venue having now been given the go-ahead, he said: "The endorsement provides additional certainty as we move into the next phase of venue planning and Games delivery, ensuring all future design and operational work continues to focus solely on Rockhampton." Saltwater crocodiles - known locally as Salties - live in both freshwater and saltwater and can grow to be in excess of six metres long. 'I'm sure all the athletes would row faster' Drew Ginn, who won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he has concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue, along with the Olympic experience for athletes and spectators at a location "six or seven hours" from Brisbane. "Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said. "I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on. "Things like relocating crocodiles out of the river, you sort of go, 'does international rowing want to have the athletes in jeopardy of that sort of stuff?'." Despite Rolland and Konietzko believing the venue will provide fair competition having reviewed the technical assessment, Ginn still has doubts. He added: "Even just the idea of being at a venue where you could have your race decided by half a second and it could show it's different in lanes by two or three seconds. "And, while I'm thinking Rockhampton is a great town, I just don't think it's right for the Olympic Games to spread the venues out in such a way that jeopardises the experience for the athletes and spectators."

item.title: Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.15
- Published The head of Microsoft AI has warned that without adequate safeguards, the development of AI could lead to the emergence of a new "silicon species" which competes with humans. Mustafa Suleyman said rival firm Anthropic is treating AI like it is human, an approach he called "misguided" which could create technology that humanity cannot control. Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, the chief executive said it was "right" for people to be concerned about AI, but there were "very practical things that we can do" to control it. The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers. Anthropic has been approached for comment. Speaking to the Today programme on Thursday, Suleyman warned against firms continuing to create AI systems capable of setting their own objectives, earning money and owning assets. That would mean "essentially seeding a new silicon species", he said, which could "no doubt compete with us for resources, no matter how much it cares about humanity and loves us". Suleyman's comments to the BBC follow an essay he published earlier this week, external, in which he questioned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude, despite praising boss Dario Amodei and his team as "intellectually honest people". In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self. He also warned tech firms risk creating something "impossible" to control by treating the technology like a human. "AIs are not conscious," he wrote. "They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations. "They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans." The Microsoft boss said greater transparency was needed around how AI systems are trained and evaluated. This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology. "We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote. Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone". 'Humanist' superintelligence The question of how much autonomy AI systems should have is increasingly dividing the industry. Speaking to the BBC about an upcoming AI summit, Suleyman called for "alignment" to create technology that must be "subordinate" to humanity. Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value. "I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and... are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity," he said. "Everybody must be aligned." Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025 and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development. Suleyman's comments reflect Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct, external, a "training manual" published on Monday for how the company is developing its AI, which sets out the idea of "humanist superintelligence". This, the code states, is "very advanced AI that always works for people, stays within limits, and remains under human control". The company's vision of a "humanist" AI highlights the central challenge facing the technology - how to make it more powerful, without losing sight of the values it is meant to serve. Additional reporting by Henry Moore

item.title: Is Canada about to join the EU?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.77
Is Canada about to join the EU? Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed European Parliament on Thursday as discussions continue to swirl about Canada's relationship with the European Union. Both sides seem to be seeking closer ties, and in his speech today, Carney said he welcomed the EU's "ambition" for Canada to become an "associate member". The president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors. US President Donald Trump has threatened to take action against the EU if it makes Canada its first "associate member". The BBC's Europe editor Katya Alder looks at the EU's future relationship with Canada and what it really means.

item.title: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.60
- Published Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher. The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war. The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen. New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week. The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis. While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks. It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping. The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday. Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand. "Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis. Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed". The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended. There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen. At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based. The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects". The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours. The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict. Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler and Benedict Garman Graphics by Tom Shiel

item.title: Is the Kennedy Center losing 'hundreds of millions of dollars'?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.43
Is the Kennedy Center losing 'hundreds of millions of dollars'? US President Donald Trump has claimed the Kennedy Center in Washington DC has been losing "tens of millions of dollars, even hundreds of millions of dollars" for years. Trump, who wants his name on the famous performing arts venue, was photographed onboard Air Force One looking at a poster with a headline that appeared to tout the demolition of the site. Federal audit records for 2024 show that, despite having "an operating deficit", it had a surplus of millions of dollars - as Aisha Sembhi explains. Design by Mesut Ersöz and Henry Esterson. Additional reporting by Tom Edgington.

item.title: US to allow Iran delegation to attend UN meetings in New York as war passes half-year mark
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.41
- Published The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the two countries grinds into its seventh month. The BBC understands the core delegation permitted to attend includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. A spokesman for the US State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products. The move comes as the war shows no sign of ending. Since it began in February, it has driven up global energy prices, and expanded into neighbouring countries. "Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week," a spokesman for the US State Department told the BBC. "The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year." Last year, diplomats attending from Iran were banned from shopping at wholesale stores like Costco. They also were required to seek permission from the US before purchasing luxury goods, including jewellery, alcohol and cars. State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott said the US would prevent the diplomats from "going on shopping sprees" as the Iranian people deal with water and electricity shortages, "brutal repression", and "soaring inflation". "We will not let the Iranian regime's elites exploit UNGA for a luxury retail splurge paid for by the Iranian people's suffering, all while the regime funnels Iran's wealth to support its terrorist proxies," he posted on X, warning New York shops to "be on guard" against selling goods to the delegation. He did not indicate if the US was aware of any specific plans from the delegation to buy luxury items. The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) is currently underway. The General Debate - the centrepiece of the annual event - is due to begin on Tuesday. Tuesday will include speeches from US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and France President Emmanuel Macron. Wednesday is expected to see speeches from the leaders of Ukraine, Syria and Iran. Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country. Since the war began, Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel. The BBC recently learned that the US denied a visa to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and the Palestinian delegation to attend UNGA. The White House, which does not recognise the legitimacy of the Palestinian delegation, denied them visas for a second year in a row.

item.title: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the same
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.41
- Published Mary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch. The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner". But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland. So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit. Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps. "It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her. They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting. 'Mary, your video is going viral' From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own. She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen". Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says. When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up". A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media." She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home. Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker. That's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, that number swells up to 80,000 each September as revellers descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world. Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand. But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out. Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night. "My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby. So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her. 'Conversation just flowed' "I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing. "Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.' "It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you." He didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out. "It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer. What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves. When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going. "It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit." They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado. She flew back to Ireland again, then he made his first trip to America for Thanksgiving 2025. Timby returned to Ireland at Christmas and met his family, and after that, they decided to make her boyfriend's big social media reveal. "We thought, this is something we already know we want to invest in... we were ready to share," Timby says. "So New Year's Eve, we shared a photo of him, and people were just over-the-moon excited." The pair watched their following grow, drawing interest from Irish cafes and tourist destinations to the local Gaelic sports club in Colorado. Their story also caught the attention of Lisdoonvarna locals, who approached Timby - a communications consultant - about being an ambassador for the festival. "So I said: Sign me up," Timby laughs. "I love the festival. It brought me Jay." Timby's been inundated with messages from lovelorn followers hoping to replicate her matchmaking success. "I heard from many of my followers... groups of people wanting to go to the festival but not having anyone to go with" or "not knowing what to do," Timby says. "I really listened to that, and I also wanted to be mindful of the fact that I love Ireland. "I'm so excited to showcase County Clare and all the amazing things that the west coast of Ireland has, but I'm also not a tour operator." So she partnered with a company called Met Through Friends, which organises and encourages real-life meetups for people looking for love. They released an interest form for a trip, expecting "80 to 100 responses." They received 560. The first group of eight will make the trip later this month, with Timby's Irish boyfriend consulting on the itinerary. "You can go on all these apps, swipe left, swipe right, but it's not actually going out and making a connection with someone and experiencing a small little town in Ireland, experiencing the culture," says Mangan. "It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience... you never know." Timby, smiling at her boyfriend of one year, agrees. "I echo everything Jay just said," she says. "Put your phone down and put yourselves out there, and good things will come."

item.title: Saudi Arabia issues first air raid alerts for Riyadh since Houthis escalated attacks
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.23
- Published Residents in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh have been given the all-clear after air raid alerts were issued and explosions were reported in the capital. It was the first time alerts have been issued in Riyadh since the Houthis increased their attacks and declared a "maritime embargo" on the Saudis in July. The Saudi Civil Defence sent alerts for the capital and several other regions late on Friday night and Saturday morning (local time) as the Kingdom's conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis continued to escalate. Journalists from Reuters and AFP reported hearing explosions in the capital, but authorities have since said the danger has passed. Residents were urged to avoid gathering in crowds. The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe. The Iran-backed group's military spokesman said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen. Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, the Houthis attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted. The attacks on Saudi oil assets have directly impacted global energy markets and the price of petrol and diesel in many countries has sharply risen in recent weeks, compounding already elevated costs caused by the blockades of the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally asked US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said. A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability." Earlier this week, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week. The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure. Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN. Additional reporting by Tabby Wilson.

item.title: Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary apologises over 'high-fare rapists' remarks
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 2.20
- Published Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has said he is "truly sorry" for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists". He had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments. O'Leary had made the remark earlier this month while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders. Following the comments, the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for an apology, in a letter seen by the BBC. O'Leary had originally said that some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe". He subsequently defended his choice of words when asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate. "British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he had added. Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime". In a video posted on Friday, O'Leary said that, over the last ten days, he had had "conversations with family and friends, both inside and outside Ryanair". "I have come to realise however that the word that I used so carelessly has caused considerable upset and offence to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors. "I want to apologise, sincerely and unreservedly, to those people, especially to the survivors." O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless", and said "it won't happen again". "I will try to learn from this mistake, and do better in future." Following O'Leary's first comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh had written to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments. She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said". She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise. "I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote. In response, O'Leary had said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape." He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training". It was not the first time O'Leary had offended people while talking about his business. In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists", external in a row over airport charges. He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories". In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws.

item.title: Kerry Kennedy: 'It would be a tragedy' if Kennedy Center is demolished

Kerry Kennedy: 'It would be a tragedy' if Kennedy Center is demolished The BBC's Caitríona Perry spoke to Kerry Kennedy, the niece of late president John F Kennedy, about demolition threats to the performance centre named after him. item.title: Amazon's big, new delivery push targets Walmart's biggest advantage, Bank of America says
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.83
Amazon's plan for more than 1,000 same-day fulfillment centers is fundamentally an attempt to close Walmart's long-held proximity advantage, Bank of America analysts wrote in a research note. Business Insider reported this week that Amazon is considering an internal project called Mercury, which would expand its same-day fulfillment network from roughly 85 facilities today to more than 1,000 by 2031. The goal is to place inventory within 10 miles of about 80% of Prime members in the US, according to internal planning documents reviewed by Business Insider. BofA analyst Justin Post said Project Mercury's strategy is less about expanding selection than making a smaller set of high-demand products more immediately accessible. Amazon's ability to compete with same-day delivery is "very important strategically," he wrote. "We see Project Mercury as another piece of Amazon's broader effort to build a denser, faster, and increasingly automated countrywide fulfillment network," Post wrote in the note. The bank called the project's estimated $6.8 billion investment "manageable" for Amazon. Internal projections reviewed by Business Insider forecast that Mercury would turn cash-flow positive by 2030 and generate $7.1 billion in economic value over 10 years. Walmart has a major head start. Its roughly 5,000 stores put fast delivery within 10 miles of 90% of the US population. The retailer has increasingly used those stores as local fulfillment centers, helping it deliver 70% of e-commerce orders the same day. Amazon's same-day sites carry a narrower assortment — roughly 90,000 fast-moving products such as paper towels, cough medicine, and fresh food — rather than the broad selection of a conventional fulfillment center. The strategy is to move those everyday purchases closer to customers without trying to replicate Amazon's full catalog in every market. The Bank of America note added that Amazon's investments in faster delivery and automation could bolster its retail profit margins for years. It cited an earlier Business Insider report on Project Tetromino, Amazon's automated delivery-station initiative. "The combination of greater network density, faster delivery, and continued automation can improve customer experience while extending the Retail margin improvement cycle for multiple years," the note said. item.title: Anthropic says Claude is now leading more than a quarter of its AI research
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.84
Claude is taking on a growing share of the work behind Anthropic's next-generation AI. Anthropic said in a Thursday blog post that Claude now "leads" 26% of its AI research and development work, meaning the chatbot can complete most of a task from a high-level prompt while a human supervises. The company said that the figure was below 1% in March. "The share of work at or above 'AI collaborates' is above 90%," Anthropic said, adding that "Claude is not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of AI R&D work." The figures could help indicate how close the industry is to recursive self-improvement, which Anthropic described as "a model fully autonomously building its successor." "Models accelerating their own development could make it more challenging for humans to understand or control these systems," Anthropic said. "It is therefore important to share these metrics to understand how close the world is to reaching recursive self improvement." Anthropic's report comes amid an ongoing debate over AI safety and how quickly the models are improving. An Anthropic researcher resigned last week and accused leading AI companies of "gambling with our lives" by pushing ahead with increasingly capable models. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has since called for frontier AI companies to coordinate on slowing development to give safety measures more time to catch up. Anthropic said in its report that the company's AI actions are reviewed by automated monitors. Anthropic said 0.002% of more than 1 billion decisions analyzed in August, which amounts to about one in 47,000, were blocked. Roughly 50 high-priority cases are escalated for human review each week. Anthropic said other frontier labs could publish the same figures and allow third parties to verify them. "We are reporting these measurements because they give the public, third parties, and governments better visibility into the pace of AI development inside frontier labs," the company said. "This means better measuring the development of AI, reporting on it publicly, and giving society an opportunity to decide how to use this information."

item.title: OpenAI takes its AI fight with Anthropic to Big Law
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.27
OpenAI is taking its seat at the counsel table. On Thursday, the company announced Astra for Law, its long-awaited offering for legal work. Lawyers have already become ChatGPT power users, but the new launch brings plugin tools, a way to search legal cases more effectively, and custom model tweaks that will help others build on the tech. As OpenAI prepares for its initial public offering, it's making a play at customers in specific industries. The legal launch marks yet another sector where OpenAI is pouring investment in its bid to become the go-to destination for AI work tools. Last week, the company unveiled ChatGPT for Financial Services, aimed at Wall Street customers. It has also launched industry-specific products for teachers, clinicians, life sciences researchers, and the personal health and finance sectors. OpenAI's launch lines up in many ways with a legal release from Anthropic, its chief rival, back in May. Both releases featured a spate of integrations, though OpenAI is also tailoring its model specifically for legal work by embedding it with tools and tweaking its settings. "You win by focusing on the customer and not the competition," said Jason Boehmig, who leads legal product at OpenAI, at a press briefing. With Astra for Law, OpenAI is targeting the legal tech industry and the 200 largest American law firms, collectively known as AmLaw 200, Boehmig said. It's built on the company's most advanced and expensive model. "What we really solved is: How do you stay on the frontier of capability, but also make the output relevant to a specific type of knowledge work," Boehmig said. Sherwin Wu, a member of the technical staff at OpenAI, said the company's model tweaks ground it in "actual case law," which led to fewer hallucinations and "just much more sound legal reasoning." The tool also gives answers that are about twice as long as typical Astra responses, the company said. "Lawyers like longer responses," Boehmig said. "That was one thing that came back from feedback." Legal tech companies like Harvey and Legora can add the tool to their own products. The launch also comes with plugins for ChatGPT from those companies, as well as from Thomson Reuters, iManage, DeepJudge, and others. Wu said that the legal product team had worked closely with the financial services team and will bring one of that launch's standout tools — a citations feature — to the legal offering soon.
