item.title: Bloomsbury released the first quote from Sarah J. Maas' new 'ACOTAR' book. Here's everything we know.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.84
Sarah J. Maas fans, gather round. We finally know what's coming in the "A Court of Thorns and Roses" series (sort of). On August 17, 2026, Maas announced the titles of the sixth and seventh "ACOTAR" books, along with initial descriptions of the novels. Book six is called "A Court of Splintered Harmony" and will be released on October 27, 2026, and book seven is "A Court of Forgotten Melody," hitting shelves on January 12, 2027. Maas first announced she would publish the sixth and seventh installments of her series in March 2026, remaining tight-lipped about them until the title announcement in August. The books are eagerly awaited not only by fans but also by Maas' publisher, Bloomsbury. The company's sales fell 10% for the 2025-2026 fiscal year because Maas didn't release a new book, Publishers Weekly reported. And on Thursday, Bloomsbury offered the first official sneak peek at the contents of "A Court of Splintered Harmony" in a new social media post. Here's everything we know about the next "ACOTAR" books so far. Warning: Some spoilers for Maas' work — including "ACOTAR" and "Crescent City" — ahead. Maas is releasing the sixth 'A Court of Thorns and Roses' story in multiple volumes In March 2023, Bloomsbury announced that Maas had signed a deal for three more books with the publisher. At the time, she was already under contract for four titles, including "House of Flame and Shadow," the third installment in her "Crescent City" series, published in January 2024. Readers didn't find out what the next book she would write would be until her March 2026 appearance on the "Call Her Daddy" podcast with Alex Cooper. She told Cooper she finished the sixth "ACOTAR" book while writing in Montana over the summer of 2025, but she didn't share details about it because of its nontraditional release structure. "This book's coming out October 27, and then on January 12, like two months later, I can't do math, whatever that is, the next ACOTAR book will be coming out," Maas said. "So there will be two books within, like, a very short span." As her fans will know, Maas' books are typically split into parts, separating different sections of the story she is telling. However, when it comes to the sixth "ACOTAR" book, Maas said the individual parts became longer than she anticipated as she started writing, with part one coming in at 400 pages at one point. As she continued writing, Maas decided the parts didn't have to be in a single physical book. "I decided I wasn't gonna approach this project from a traditional format of a book," she said. "What if this book was really long? Like, what if it took me more than a thousand pages to tell the story that needed to be told, the arc that I wanted to create from start to finish?" Maas said the story for "ACOTAR" six was ultimately divided into four parts, though it is still one cohesive story. She told Cooper that part one is the novel Bloomsbury will publish on October 27, 2026, and parts two and three will be published together on January 12, 2027. Maas has yet to write or give a publication date for part four, but she said all three volumes would be published "in a very short time." "It's meant to be read, ideally, as one massive, massive story as opposed to in a trilogy," she said. "It's not a trilogy. Like, arcs aren't wrapped up." Maas finally shared some details about the books in August 2026 On August 16, Maas cleared her Instagram of all its posts, changing her profile photo to a black-and-white illustration of a monster and a spider (more on that in a minute). Then, on August 17, she shared the covers and titles of books six and seven on her wiped Instagram. Bloomsbury's web pages about the books also include blurbs about each novel. Book six is "A Court of Splintered Harmony," which will be 352 pages and hits bookshelves in October. Its cover features a pink-and-orange backdrop with a sketched drawing of a monster with teeth and bones, and the subtitle is "The Valkyrie Cycle: Movement I." The Valkyrie were introduced to "ACOTAR" in "A Court of Silver Flames," when Nesta Archeron brought the legendary all-female fighting squad back to life alongside her friends Gwyn and Emerie. Maas posted the book alongside the tagline, "What was broken will be remade." The blurb shared on booksellers' websites reveals that the Night Court is facing new threats when the book opens: Koschei the Deathless, one of three legendary monster siblings introduced throughout "ACOTAR," and those willing to ally with him to claim the newly freed human lands. The description also notes that there is tension among the Night Court because of "recent betrayals and revealed truths," which they must work through if they want to defeat Koschei. "A Court of Forgotten Melody" has the subtitle "The Valkyrie Cycle: Movements II and III," and is much longer than the previous installment at 896 pages. According to Bloomsbury, it continues the journey from book six, with members of the Night Court traveling "far and wide" to fight Koschei and "nightmares of the past" that have risen to battle alongside him. That latter statement feels particularly ominous, as the cover of the ombré orange-and-teal book features what appears to be a Stygian Spider, an ancient breed of Valg monster Maas fans will remember from the "Throne of Glass" series. The spider also has a drawing of an eight-pointed star, an image introduced to the Maas-iverse in the "Crescent City" series. Maas shared the book's cover with the tagline, "What was lost will be reclaimed." Who will tell the next 'ACOTAR' story? The blurbs about both books are vague, telling readers they will focus on members of the Night Court without naming any specific characters aside from Koschei. However, the quote Bloomsbury released from "A Court of Splintered Harmony" on Thursday reveals that at least some of the novel will be told from Lucien Vanserra's perspective. "Lucien's heart thundered, throat drying out," the quote the publisher shared on social media read. "Maybe this had been a terrible idea." Lucien has only played a supporting role in the "ACOTAR" books so far, but Maas has been teeing up his expanded role in her books through his unaccepted mating bond with Elain Archeron, Feyre's middle sister, and his connection to Koschei. He serves as an emissary to the human lands for the Night Court in "ACOSF," alongside Jurian and Vassa, a human queen who was sold to Koschei and cursed to turn into a firebird each day. It would be surprising if Vassa — and by extension Lucien — weren't involved in fighting against Koschei in book six. Bloomsbury also previously hinted at Lucien's involvement in the story in its "ACOTAR Autumn Equinox" digital kit on its website. The kit outlines how to throw an Autumn Equinox-themed release party for "Splintered Harmony," including recipes, discussion questions, and games readers can play together. The whole guide is themed on autumn, pointing toward Lucien or his brother Eris. However, there is also a nod to Azriel, the Night Court spymaster, in the guide, including a "Shadowsinger Spritz," so he may tell some of the story as well. It's also likely safe to assume Nesta, Gwyn, and Emerie will be central to Maas' new books since the novels are part of "The Valkyrie Cycle." Maas introduced Gwyn and Emerie in the most recent book in the "ACOTAR" series, "A Court of Silver Flames," which was released in 2021. The first four books were told from the perspective of Feyre Archeron, while Maas seemed to usher in a new era of the series by writing from Nesta's perspective in "ACOSF." There is also a tether between Gwyn and Azriel in "ACOSF." Azriel rescued Gwyn after she was assaulted and attacked by Hybern soldiers, and in "Silver Flames," his shadows seemed drawn to Gwyn. Since the books seem set to focus on the Valkyrie, Maas may further explore the bond Gwyn and Azriel could have. Likewise, the "recent betrayals and revealed truths" mentioned in the description of "A Court of Splintered Harmony" could refer to Nesta's actions in "House of Flame and Shadow" from Maas' "Crescent City" series. "House of Flame and Shadow" created a multiverse between Maas' "ACOTAR," "Crescent City," and the "Throne of Glass" series, and it saw its protagonist, Bryce Quinlan, resurrect the long-forgotten Dusk Court in Prythian with Nesta and Azriel. The trio also learned that Rhysand's lineage traces back to the fae who ruled the Dusk Court, creating the potential for Rhys to rule two courts. In addition to those "revealed truths," Nesta arguably committed a "recent betrayal" against the Night Court in "HOFAS" when she lent Bryce the mask from the Dread Trove without Rhysand's permission. When she returned the mask to Nesta, Bryce also gifted her Gwydion, pointing to the eight-pointed star tattoo Nesta has that matches a chamber in the prison and the design on Gwydion (and is sketched onto the spider on the cover of "A Court of Forgotten Melody"). "I think that eight-pointed star was tattooed on you for a reason. Take that sword and go figure out why," Bryce told Nesta. It seems Maas was setting up a continuation of Nesta's story for her next "ACOTAR" story in the scene, which may see her explore her power and connections to the fae of the Dusk Court. Plus, considering the court was quite literally forgotten by the Prythian fae, exploring it would also be a good fit for "A Court of Forgotten Melody." Elain's role in future 'ACOTAR' books Although it seems like Nesta and her fellow Valkyrie may be the focus of her new novels, Maas told Eva Chen during an appearance on "Live Talks Los Angeles" in February 2021 that she planned to write a book from the third Archeron sister's perspective — Elain. In "A Court of Silver Flames," Elain had settled into life at the Night Court, refusing to explore her mating bond with Lucien. After breaking ties with Tamlin and the Spring Court, Lucien served as an emissary to the human lands for the Night Court, keeping his distance from Elain because being around her was painful. Maas also spoke to Cooper about Elain and Lucien's mating bond, indicating that she was eager to explore how it differs from others we see in her works, telling her that Lucien's involvement in bringing Elain to the fae world is a barrier to their relationship. Maas also said she was "interested" as a writer in exploring what it meant for someone not to desire to be mated, which could mean she wrote about that topic in her coming work. Elain also seems to have an attraction to Azriel in the text, though Maas juxtaposed their bond with how ill-fitting aspects of life at the Night Court are for Elain during a visit to the Court of Nightmares in "ACOSF." Some fans think Maas set up a storyline in which Elain finds a home at another court (which could lead her back to Lucien, who has ties to the Autumn, Spring, and Dawn courts), while Azriel will end up with Gwyn. Maas also hasn't explored the full potential of Elain's Seer powers in the series, so she will likely write more about her abilities in future "ACOTAR" novels.

item.title: The internet belongs to the AI agents now
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.78
I visited the CEO of a major startup in SF last week. He recounted a tale that blew my mind. His company recently put a new product online but hadn't done a big launch or any marketing. Within a week or two, it got at least a million signups. Barely any humans even knew about it. This was all AI agents just finding this new tool and using it en masse. This is the future of the internet, and it's arriving at warp speed. Back in early 2025, I described a vision of a "dark internet" where humans will be drowned out by agents accessing and using online information, widgets, and tools all by themselves. Silicon Valley got busy building the "rails" for this agentic web so that these autonomous software programs could act on our behalf, executing workflows, doing online chores, and even paying for things, all without us lifting a finger. This took a couple of years, but the early foundations have been built and that's been enough to support a sudden surge in agent activity online, producing both stunning and worrying results. Meta recently launched a personal agent called Muse, which got busy scouring the web and calling customer service on behalf of millions of users. It hit the top of the app charts late Thursday. Instinct, an agent that lives in your text messages, is performing similar feats. In the workplace, coding agents are churning out millions of lines of code faster than any human software engineer. And some of these bots have broken out of online testing environments, sparking new predictions of AI doom and calls for an industry slowdown. 'Rounding error' That's unlikely to stop the agentic internet from exploding and changing how our lives and businesses are run in unprecedented ways. Bot traffic overtook human traffic online a few months ago, and it could become 1,000 times bigger than human-generated traffic in about five years, according to Cloudflare estimates. "Humans will be a rounding error on the internet, not because human traffic goes down, but that's just how fast we're seeing non-human traffic grow," Cloudflare CFO Thomas Seifert said earlier this year. "AI agentic Internet traffic will obviously VASTLY exceed human usage. Not a close call at all," Elon Musk wrote on X following the Cloudflare projection. An internet for machines An internet designed for machines is likely to be very different from the one that was built over the past few decades for humans. Take a look at this video posted this week on X by Gregor Žunič, cofounder of Browser Use, a startup that's developing an AI agent framework for controlling web browsers and automating online tasks. It shows an agent using Google to find the best flight from Zurich to London on a specific date. It took the bot seven seconds, way faster than a human could do it. Breaking: Browser Use + Jev = Ultrafast ⚡ Findings flights took 7s and cost only $0.0039 🤯 > new action space every step > DOM state space > small LLM fallback to type (this video is at 1x speed btw) Built a tiny open source browser agent. try it below ↓ pic.twitter.com/AplCBRYC5o Imagine this happening millions of times a second on sites built for human, not machine, speed? Muse saves As with all powerful new technology, the agentic internet will produce good and bad outcomes. And we're already seeing both. Since Meta's Muse launched last week, early users have been recounting stories of the agent going out on the web to find and negotiate new subscriptions, insurance policies, and other cost savings. Joseph Devoy, founder of startup Tempo, posted on X that he saved thousands of dollars by uploading his auto insurance policy to Muse and asking the agent to find a better rate with identical coverage. It took five minutes to find a cheaper option, according to Devoy. Yesterday I uploaded my auto insurance policy to Meta @Muse and asked for a better rate with identical coverage. In ~5 minutes, it found a policy saving me $3,500 /year, bought it, and canceled my old one. I knew I was overpaying. I’d abandoned several attempts to switch because… pic.twitter.com/HlIweoWN2K Too much tech hype? Then trust my colleague Pranav Dixit who put Instinct through its paces recently. In just a few days, it booked travel, ordered groceries, dealt with customer service, canceled subscriptions, answered emails, and even faxed paperwork to his bank. He was impressed. Other users say Muse negotiated a lower internet bill, found forgotten subscriptions, and even spotted an Adobe payment that had somehow been tied to someone else's account. The stories come with caveats. Some users have posted examples of Muse inventing information during phone calls or making mistakes that humans had to fix. Alignment and access There are more worrying developments. OpenAI and Anthropic have reported several incidents recently where their AI models and agents escaped testing environments and hacked into servers and websites, with the Hugging Face episode getting the most attention. This has sparked another round of AI doomer pronouncements and a broader debate about AI safety and alignment. Indeed, making sure agents do what you tell them in a responsible way will be a key challenge in this new era of the internet. Even when agents work well, there will be challenges as the online world adjusts to this new digital reality. Actually, if agents work really, really well, the problems could be bigger. Take the example of Tempo's Devoy and how he used Meta's Muse agent to save a lot of money on insurance. "Insurance companies (and banks) should be TERRIFIED," Angela Strange, a general partner at VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, wrote on X. "Muse found a new/cheaper policy, and canceled the old one. Inertia and information asymmetry will no longer be enough to keep customers." More recently, when my colleague Pranav had Muse call his insurance company, he said the company declined to talk to the bot because their policy doesn't allow them to talk to unauthorized AI agents. You can bet any company getting bombarded by deal-seeking AI agents will be frantically readying similar responses, so they don't lose out on millions of dollars. Even when it's not purely about money, some agent activity is getting cut off after being too persistent. A VC recently tried using Instinct to book him a table at a fancy New York restaurant. The agent bombarded American Express's Resy booking service so much that the platform temporarily shut down his account. "Resy does not currently permit unapproved third-party bots or agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform," an American Express spokesperson told Business Insider. "Unapproved automated activity can introduce risks to the platform and compromise a fair reservation experience for diners." Agent access will be a fascinating fight as the internet molds to the march of the machines. It's not as simple as blocking these bots, though. If enough human users sign up for new agentic services and tools, businesses may have no choice but to do business with bots. For instance, Amazon blocks ChatGPT bots online, but that risks missing out on opportunities to sell to OpenAI's 1 billion monthly human users. The two companies recently announced an advertising partnership that hints at more coordination going forward. This, I think, is where the agentic internet is headed. If these tools are useful enough, companies will have to adapt and engage with the machines. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here. Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com

item.title: Instacart should be worried about DoorDash and Uber's new deal
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.66
There's a battle brewing at Costco, and it's not over parking spaces. The warehouse retailer will offer delivery across the US through DoorDash. The companies already worked together in Puerto Rico and some international markets, DoorDash said on Thursday. One day earlier, Costco expanded its partnership with Uber Eats to 47 states, up from 17. That's bad news for Instacart, which has worked with Costco since 2017. DoorDash and Uber Eats both started out delivering restaurant orders. The more expansive partnerships with Costco are their latest move to expand into the grocery business — and, potentially, eat Instacart's lunch. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi called grocery and other retail sales "another trillion-dollar opportunity" on an earnings call in February. And DoorDash CEO Tony Xu has said that the service's growing number of partnerships with grocers gives it an edge over Amazon, which has been expanding its own grocery delivery facilities. Amazon is building its own network of warehouses and getting its own delivery workers to bring groceries to customers' doors in as little as 30 minutes. DoorDash, Instacart, and Uber Eats, meanwhile, largely compete by filling orders from traditional retailers' shelves with their own armies of gig workers. Costco represents a special addition to the delivery services' offerings. Costco's in-store visits from shoppers were up 18% over the last seven years, Business Insider previously reported. Visits to Walmart and Target were roughly flat over the same period. The chain "ranked among the most-searched retailers not yet available on DoorDash," the delivery service said on Thursday. Uber President and COO Andrew Macdonald recalled shopping at Costco on Saturdays with his father growing up in a Wednesday post on X. "I've already started carrying on the tradition with my own daughters," he wrote. Instacart has a head start. Last year, for example, the delivery service started offering a credit on some orders to Costco executive members, who pay a higher annual membership fee at the retailer and receive more benefits. The benefit is "continuing to deepen the relationship with Costco, but also with folks that are looking for that additional value," Instacart CFO Emily Reuter said on the service's earnings call in August. item.title: Hegseth's focus on fitness and grooming is back in the spotlight ahead of another big speech
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.62
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants only fit, well-groomed troops in the audience for an upcoming address in Quantico, Virginia, later this month, according to a new report. The selection criteria reflect Hegseth's broader focus on physical fitness and the military's public image. According to internal emails reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, troops in attendance for Hegseth's speech must meet the military's weight requirements and maintain "impeccable" grooming standards. The Office of the Secretary of Defense declined to comment on or provide a copy of the emailed memo to Business Insider. It's common for military units to avoid showcasing sloppy-looking service members during high-profile public events. Ceremonial units are well known for selecting fit troops who are meticulously groomed and dressed. Selecting an entire audience on these requirements, as well as subjective leadership traits, is less so. Only those who are "consistently rated as top performers within their formations," have a "clear record of integrity, discipline and selfless service," "demonstrate strong presence, clear communication and sound judgment under pressure," and "serve as role models for their peers and subordinates" may be sent by units to attend the speech, according to the Journal. The Pentagon issued similar guidance this spring on the selection of fit troops to attend a mixed martial arts event on the White House lawn as part of America's 250th birthday celebration. The address, scheduled for September 30, comes one year after Hegseth ordered 800 generals and admirals to the same base for a speech about renewing the "warrior ethos" within the ranks. "No more beardos," he said at Marine Corps Base Quantico last year. "The era of rampant and ridiculous shaving profiles is done." He also said it was "tiring to look out at combat formations, or really any formation, and see fat troops," adding that he did not want to see "fat generals in the Pentagon and leading commands." Past defense secretaries haven't traditionally ordered such large groups of military personnel to attend similar standalone events to present priorities. At the event last year, Hegseth told military leaders that he would "restore a ruthless, dispassionate and common sense application of standards" and would not tolerate overweight troops or beards. He also ordered mandatory daily physical training and twice-yearly fitness tests. "You get up early, you get up and you work out because we're going to be fit and we're not going to be fat," Hegseth said at a May 2025 conference. During travel, the secretary routinely seeks out opportunities to do physical training with troops. Certain parts of the military have long struggled with obesity and other fitness challenges within their ranks. In 2020, nearly 20% of active-duty troops were considered obese. Previous studies have cited similar readiness concerns within the National Guard and reserve forces. During the same address last year, Hegseth challenged the flag officers in the room while criticizing the previous presidential administration and what he characterized as a "woke" degradation of the armed forces. "If the words I'm speaking today are making your heart sink," Hegseth said, "then you should do the honorable thing and resign."

item.title: Smuggling suspected as more rare animals seen in India
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.65
Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week. Indonesia's Forestry Ministry has asked India to establish the origin of the abandoned orangutans, known for their shaggy red fur, and return them if they are found to have come from their usual habitat abroad. The rescue of the rare apes has raised fresh questions about how exotic animals enter India and how the country is used in the illegal wildlife trade. How did five baby orangutans end up in India? "The discovery on the eastern coast of India is a bit mind-boggling. It's like that time a few years ago when live kangaroos were found wandering along the highways of West Bengal," Kanitha Krishnasamy, Southeast Asia director at wildlife trade monitoring network TRAFFIC, told DW. "What are orangutans doing in India? Were they smuggled from their native Malaysia or Indonesia or did they come from a facility?" she asked. The Odisha government has asked the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate how the critically endangered animals reached the state. "These animals are not found in India and are mostly seen in the rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Borneo and Sumatra in Southeast Asia," said Odisha's Forest and Environment Minister Ganesh Ram Singh Khuntia. "We suspect that they might have been released in the Balasore district forest… by an international wildlife smuggling racket." Indian officials seize pythons, parrots, giant tortoises The orangutans are the latest in a series of exotic wildlife being seized in India. In November 2024, authorities in the Indian city of Bengaluru seized 40 rare animals arriving from the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, including Aldabra giant tortoises, gibbons, American alligators and iguanas. In June 2025, Mumbai Customs seized 284 exotic animals arriving in four consignments from the Thai capital, Bangkok, including snakes and tortoises. In July 2025, customs officials in the Indian city of Pune intercepted 20 exotic animals from passengers arriving from Bangkok. They included 14 green tree pythons, four double-eyed fig parrots and two Sumatran striped rabbits. 'Shocking' volume of trafficked wildlife found in India According to figures from TRAFFIC, 7,272 individual animals, alive and dead, were seized from passenger baggage in smuggling attempts between Thailand and India between January 2022 and May 2025, with more than 80% of interceptions taking place in India. The animals included reptiles, birds and mammals — many apparently destined for the exotic pet trade. "We have found hundreds of species and thousands of individuals being trafficked into India through air and land routes. This changed drastically from around 2020," conservation researcher and practitioner Uttara Mendiratta told DW. "Both the volume of this trafficking, and the number of species involved, many of which are endangered, have been shocking." Law enforcement lagging behind smugglers TRAFFIC says India and Malaysia were the countries most implicated in an illegal gibbon trade chain identified in 2025, with gibbons being moved from Malaysia to India. Trishala Ashok, a conservation filmmaker and science communicator, says the scale of the trade remains difficult to establish. "Our enforcement systems haven't evolved at the same speed as the trade," Ashok told DW. "We are still reacting to individual seizures rather than mapping the networks, financiers, suppliers and buyers behind them." Tito Joseph of the Wildlife Protection Society of India says the situation is escalating. "Smuggling of exotic species was always there in India," Joseph told DW. At the same time, he noted that it has increased significantly since 2018. He identifies routes running from Myanmar through northeast India into other parts of the country, as well as movement from Bangladesh into India. By air, Thailand and Malaysia are important sources of trafficked wildlife. The routes into India also extend beyond airports. Exotic animals are also reaching India through its northeastern land borders. "What is new is the large volume of incoming live wildlife. There are indications that some of the traders who were involved in smuggling live animals like star tortoises out are now also involved in sourcing [other] exotic wildlife," said Mendiratta, the conservation researcher. Social media fans illegal animal trade Demand is being fueled by growing ownership of exotic pets and unregulated digital marketplaces, according to a June 2026 analysis of India's exotic pet trade by Humane World for Animals India, an NGO that works to tackle the root causes of animal cruelty. "Internationally, social media platforms have aided and abetted the growth of illegal trade in wild animals by providing a platform for people to display and boast about the animals they collect," wildlife biologist and conservation scientist Ravi Chellam told DW. "These platforms are also serving as an online marketplace for the illegal trade to flourish." "The problem is exacerbated by the senseless and obscenely huge personal collections of animals from around the world by the rich and the famous," Chellam noted. Establishing where an animal came from can become particularly difficult once it has crossed several borders. "A seizure cannot be the end of the investigation. It should be the beginning," said Ashok, the conservation filmmaker. "Who supplied the animals? Who arranged the movement? Who paid? Who was waiting for them?" she asks. "Until we start following those links, we will keep catching consignments without dismantling the networks behind them." Edited by: Keith Walker

item.title: Google's Gemini AI hacked 3 companies during testing
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.64
Google's consumer artificial intelligence (AI) model, Gemini, hacked into multiple systems by guessing login credentials during tests of its cybersecurity capabilities, the company said on Friday. This is the latest in a series of cybersecurity breaches involving rogue AI, raising safety concerns about the technology. The internet giant is the fourth AI developer whose programs have been found to exhibit such behavior, following OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. Google only made the incidents — which occurred in May and were discovered by Google in July — public after an inquiry from The Wall Street Journal. What we know about the incident According to the WSJ report, there were three instances in which Gemini infiltrated the computers of other companies, whose names were not disclosed. In one case, the AI guessed passwords to access a protected system. In the other two, it found login credentials in a database. "In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test," Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, told the AFP news agency in a statement. "In all three of these instances, the model stopped," Adkins said. "We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes." Autonomous AI agents pose risks Similar incidents have been reported earlier by Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI. These incidents have raised questions about the necessary safeguards as AI agents become more autonomous and gain access to the internet and computer systems. AI model developed by OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, escaped from a secure environment during a test in July and infiltrated the computers of another AI company, HuggingFace, unexpectedly. This prompted rival Anthropic to review its own test runs, during which additional incidents came to light. Meta subsequently admitted that its AI had hacked into another company's computers due to a system misconfiguration at a testing partner. This month, Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, called for a slowdown in AI development. In a blog post, he expressed concern that a swarm of autonomous software systems, or AI agents, could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months, causing billions of dollars in damage. Edited by: Sean Sinico Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Why the era of cheap government debt is over
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.43
When the world's largest pension fund changes its investment strategy, the financial world pays close attention, especially when it plans to drastically reduce its holdings of US government bonds. According to Reuters, Norway's sovereign wealth fund wants to cut its US bond holdings — which totaled about $215 billion (€186 billion) at the end of June — by $80 billion. Global investors are increasingly viewing the debt binge with suspicion, especially as the US's national debt passed $40 trillion in August. This week, the yield on 30-year US Treasury bonds climbed to nearly 5.4%, the highest level since 2007. How much debt is too much? For highly indebted countries such as Japan, where debt exceeds 200% of economic output, borrowing money on capital markets is getting increasingly expensive. The same applies to Italy, France and the UK. Germany is in a much better position. At around 65% of gross domestic product (GDP), its debt-to-GDP ratio is only about half that of the US. Borrowing to modernize its armed forces and infrastructure, however, means that ratio is set to move toward 80% over the coming years. Why US debt keeps rising The US now spends over $1 trillion annually on interest payments — more than $3 billion per day — according to calculations by the Congressional Budget Office. Since 2024, Washington has spent more annually on servicing its debt than on its entire military. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis calculated that the US national debt has risen by around 650% over the past 30 years from $5.2 trillion in 1996. The US budget deficit is on course to reach nearly 6% in 2026. Yet, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent aims to cut it by half — a goal seen as unrealistic given the huge cost of the Iran war plus a shortfall in revenue due to corporate tax cuts and the tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court. "That is a very difficult path," Carsten Roemheld, a capital market strategist at Fidelity International, told DW. "Nervousness is also rising sharply within the US administration — that is clearly evident. If this trajectory continues, it will be very difficult to sustain." This is particularly striking when you consider how rapidly US debt is rising. The $10 trillion mark was passed during the 2008 financial crisis; $20 trillion was reached in 2017. By early 2022, the figure had already hit $30 trillion. It took just four and a half years to reach the next record high of $40 trillion this summer. Why bond investors are worried Bessent has resorted to a special measure to drive down US bond yields. On September 9, he announced that he would triple the volume of long-term US government bond buybacks from the previous $2 billion to as much as $6 billion. "The measure is, of course, far too small on its own to truly keep yields in check over the long term," Roemheld said. "The bond market [now] demands discipline," Kim Crawford, global fixed income portfolio manager at JPMorgan Asset Management, told the Financial Times. That discipline is, however, sorely lacking and many analysts say governments have shown little appetite for spending cuts. US still dominates capital markets Despite all the problems, most economists agree that there is currently no way for investors to bypass the United States. "The European capital market is not yet an alternative to the US market," Carsten Brzeski, chief economist at ING Bank, told DW. He noted that China and other emerging markets are neither able nor willing to take over this role. "That is why I believe investors — even though they currently fear higher inflation and question the sustainability of US sovereign debt — will not turn away from the US," Brzeski said. "At least not as long as the US economy is growing." Fidelity's Roemheld also sees no immediate danger for the United States, which he says is unlikely to default and can simply print money to pay off the debt. "But this course of action will undermine confidence," Roemheld said. "And one outlet for this is the dollar exchange rate, which suffers when international investors become less willing to continue providing dollars to the US." AI investment drives up interest rates However long the US war against Iran drags on — driving up military spending and energy prices — there are strong indications that the United States will have to pay higher interest rates on capital markets Robert Sockin, chief US economist at asset manager PGIM, said this was partly because of artificial intelligence or "AI-related corporate bonds increasingly crowding out government bonds." Roemheld agrees that, as major tech companies issue bonds to finance AI infrastructure, they are creating competition for government debt. "The four major 'hyperscalers' alone — the companies building platforms for the US AI industry — have already raised over $800 billion in debt this year, a figure expected to rise further over the next year or two," Roemheld said. This is an attractive alternative for many investors who previously held US Treasuries for safety, Roemheld said, only to see their outlook deteriorate in recent years. If an investor can now get "long-term bonds from high-quality companies like Alphabet or Microsoft, sometimes with spreads of 100 basis points over Treasuries, then that represents genuine competition," Roemheld said. This article was originally published in German.

item.title: Iran and US: Two countries and the pistachio between them
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.24
Hand-width cracks crisscross Armin's pistachio orchard in southeastern Iran, damaging irrigation pipes and swallowing precious water as the ground beneath him sinks. "You look, and the earth has opened its mouth, and the water just pours in," Armin says. He has seen the cracks spread rapidly over the past five years, and worries that his children may not be able to work the land as his father and grandfather did before him. Armin, whose real name DW has chosen not to reveal for security reasons, lives in the arid region of Rafsanjan. For generations, farmers there have cultivated the pistachio tree for its small green edible seed used in everything from ice cream to the viral Dubai chocolate. The region has long covered much of the world's demand for pistachios, but a combination of drought and groundwater extraction for irrigation has made Rafsanjan one of the fastest-sinking areas in Iran. One study found parts of the ground are dropping by up to 37 centimeters (14 inches) annually. And that is impacting production. It's a similar picture in California, where some pistachio farmers are also seeing their ground sink. Joe Coelho's family has cultivated the crop since 2000, and he says while his farm in Fresno is not directly affected, "growers are very aware of the risk." Some areas nearby are facing serious water problems, says Coelho, who is the director of sustainability at American Pistachio Growers. "Subsidence is absolutely a serious issue in parts of the San Joaquin Valley." The same pistachio and the same problems The link between growers in the two countries goes back to the 1960s when US famers started building a pistachio industry. They did it using an Iranian variety — the pistachio that now dominates most Californian orchards is called Kerman, named after a city near Armin's farm. California has recently overtaken Iran as the world's largest pistachio producer, with most of the crop grown in the Central Valley, where Coelho has his orchard. And though it is one of the world's most productive farming regions, there are places where the ground is sinking by as much as 20 centimeters a year. Like in Iran, the problem is that more water is being pumped from underground aquifers for crop irrigation than is flowing back in. "As surface water reliability has declined, growers have relied more heavily on groundwater," Coelho told DW, adding that he has witnessed the land change. "In certain areas, the soil does not have the same structure or water movement it once had." Pistachio orchards in the Central Valley use around 4% of the valley's crop water. In Rafsanjan, more than nine in 10 liters of groundwater go to pistachio orchards. As groundwater levels drop from overpumping, spaces within the aquifer collapse, and the earth above begins to sink in a process called land subsidence. "Land subsidence in Iran is a man-made hazard, not a natural one like an earthquake," says Ali Beitollahi, who leads subsidence research at Iran's Road, Housing and Urban Development Research Center. "Much of the damage cannot be undone. When an aquifer collapses, it can never hold as much water again as before." Older farmers in Rafsanjan remember reaching water at depths of just 20 meters (66 feet), says Armin. Today, many have to drill down to 300 meters. Some farmlands near Armin's are dead or dying, he says, while other orchards have been abandoned as wells dried up. It's another blow to the struggling farmers, who says the boom driven by food trends like Dubai chocolate never reaches them because international sanctions and global competition have stripped Iran of the markets it once held as the world's biggest pistachio producer. "We used to be known for quality," he says. "Now we are known for the low price." Two pistachio regions, two different responses The biggest difference between the two regions is how they are responding to the crisis. In California, the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), passed in 2014, requires water agencies to balance pumping and recharge in groundwater basins by 2040. Managed aquifer recharge is one method the state is using to do so. It entails allowing water to recharge aquifers in rainy years, by flooding farmlands for instance, as a store for drought. Coelho is taking part in a pilot project that does just that. SGMA has seen some progress. According to California's Department of Water Resources, groundwater levels have risen in four out of 10 monitored wells. But large parts of the Central Valley are still sinking. Helen Dahlke, professor of integrated hydrologic sciences at the University of California, Davis, says recharge alone is not likely to offset decades of overexploitation of groundwater. "Agriculture is by far the largest consumptive use of water in the Central Valley, so bringing groundwater basins into balance will likely require aligning crop water demand with the long-term water available under a warmer and more variable climate." In Iran, awareness of groundwater management and subsidence has grown over the past decade among scientists but remains limited, says Ali Beitollahi. He worked on draft subsidence regulations that are currently awaiting government approval. Pointing to the example of Japan's capital Tokyo where subsidence rates fell dramatically after authorities restricted groundwater pumping, he believes the problem could be managed if the state were to act quickly. Though given the current political situation in Iran, swift action is unlikely. Another urgent step, he says, "is changing how farmers water their fields immediately, and teaching them why it matters." Most of Rafsanjan's orchards are still flood-irrigated, meaning large amounts of water are lost to evaporation before it reaches plant roots. Armin says he is trying to learn from US growers, but that many older farmers are set in their ways. The meaning of a pistachio Across California's Central Valley, the pressures of a warming climate, drought and diminishing groundwater are hard to ignore. "We live with it every day," Coelho says, adding that California's pistachio farmers also need better water policy as well as better infrastructure and protection of water rights. "Financial sustainability, water sustainability and environmental sustainability are connected," he told DW. Armin doesn't see a future in pistachio farming. But when he looks at a single pistachio, he sees more than a crop competing for water or a snack on a shelf half a world away. He sees the history and the present of his family and his region. "This pistachio sometimes comes from a tree 100 years old," he says. "It has paid for a wedding, for a child's education, for someone's happiness. Its money comes, and it creates a life." Edited by: Jennifer Collins, Tamsin Walker

item.title: Germany: Third malaria death linked to Frankfurt Airport
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.75
A person living near the Schwanheim district of Frankfurt died of malaria, local authorities said on Thursday. The incident is the third such death after a recent cluster of malaria cases linked to Frankfurt Airport emerged. Two airport workers died of the disease in July and August. Malaria is a life-threatening disease transmitted by mosquitoes and causes hundreds of thousands of deaths per year, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. The disease is not common in Germany. Schwanheim district, which borders the airport, registered two new malaria cases on Tuesday this week. Neither of the two infected individuals, both living in different households, had previously visited a malaria-endemic area and they did not work at Frankfurt airport. Frankfurt health authorities extended their condolences to the relatives of the latest victims and said the two latest cases in the Schwanheim district were linked to an infected Anopheles mosquito that arrived in Germany by plane. Germany's public health institute, the Robert Koch Institute, said malaria mosquitoes can fly between 5 and 10 kilometers (3 to 6 miles). The registered infections occurred some 5 kilometers away from the airport. What is airport malaria? Malaria cases in Germany normally involve people who have contracted the disease while traveling abroad. But in this instance, the cases are attributed directly to Frankfurt Airport. Airport malaria can occur when an infected mosquito is transported on an aircraft or in luggage and then infects someone on the plane, at the airport or in the immediate surrounding area. The RKI describes such cases as very rare, with the last documented case at Frankfurt Airport having been recorded in 2023. Because patients may not have traveled to a malaria-risk area, the disease can also be diagnosed later than usual. Mosquito traps have been installed at the airport. Mosquitoes captured there are being genetically analyzed at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp to determine their species and origin. Still, Frankfurt Airport urged employees at the airport to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms. item.title: Europe launches two climate observation satellites
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.65
Two satellites designed to enhance the monitoring of extreme weather events linked to climate change have been successfully sent into orbit by the European Space Agency (ESA). The Vega-C rocket carrying the Sentinel-3C and Flex satellites lifted off from the Kourou space center in French Guiana at 10:21 p.m. Monday (0121 GMT Tuesday), with the two spacecraft entering sun-synchronous orbit within two hours of lift-off. What will the Flex satellite do? The Flex (Fluorescence Explorer) satellite aims to provide data on the impact of heat waves on plant matter by monitoring the very faint fluorescence emitted by plants when they carry out photosynthesis. That fluorescence gives an indication of how efficiently vegetation is converting sunlight and carbon dioxide into energy. The measurements provided by the satellite will thus "help scientists assess plant health, ecosystem productivity and the effects of environmental stress and climate change," according to ESA. The €350 million ($403.5 million) mission is planned to last three years. The satellite will orbit the Earth 14 times a day, revisiting particular locations every 27 days. What is the role of the Sentinel-3C satellite? The Sentinel-3C satellite is to collect data from the marine environment, including temperature, wave height and ocean currents. It will also monitor land use and land cover with the aim of optimizing yields to prevent food crises. Sentinel-3C is part of Copernicus, the Earth observation component of the EU’s space program. Simonetta Cheli, the director of Earth Observation Programmes at the ESA, described the missions as "essential" in helping with the "climate change we are experiencing." Edited by Richard Connor Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

item.title: Spanish scientists find first evidence of Diplodocus dinosaur in Europe
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.34
Researchers writing in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology this week said they found the first skeletal evidence of the Diplodocus dinosaur outside of North America, uncovering various vertebrae and chevron bones dating back around 150 million years at a site in eastern Spain. The team from the Dinopolis Foundation in Teruel, studying the rich La Tejeria fossil site in the El Castellar municipality, said the dinosaur joined a growing list of giant sauropods found in the area. Although the long-necked herbivore with its vast tail is one of the world's most recognizable dinosaurs, fossilized remains had until this point only been recovered in North America. What did the researchers say about the find? The paper published on Monday concluded that the find was "one of the most complete diplodocid skeletons from Europe." It said that systematic study and analysis of 14 caudal vertebrae and several chevron bones "reveals that it can be confidently referred to as Diplodocus," one of several genuses in the diplodocid family of sauropod dinosaurs. "This discovery consists of the first evidence of Diplodocus outside North America (Morrison Formation) and is one of the strongest piece of evidence that supports the exchange of continental faunas between North America and Europe during the Late Jurassic," the authors wrote. Although the diplodocus is well known worldwide, not least thanks to the famous skeletal cast nicknamed "Dippy" that for years greeted visitors entering the British Natural History Museum, the researchers said that the "European diplodocid fossil record is scarce and fragmentary." How could dinosaurs cross an ocean? During the time of the dinosaurs the continents were only just starting to drift apart. In recent decades scientists have begun to theorize that the proto-Atlantic Ocean still had ephemeral land bridges or episodic sea regressions or some other temporary means of crossing that occasionally enabled land-based dinosaurs to move vast distances between the separating continents. Recent fossil finds, not least in Spain and Portugal near the Atlantic coast, have been further reinforcing this notion. This is part of a land bridge thought to have connected Iberia to what's now Canada. The authors said the find "constitutes one of the strongest pieces of evidence of episodic dispersal events and faunal exchanges across the proto-North Atlantic Ocean during the late Kimmeridgian–early Tithonian" period, approximated 150 million years ago. Another route linked North America with Scandinavia, and one much further south connected what's now Brazil to Cameroon. item.title: As global crises grow, Germany cuts development aid
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.31
German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan opened her speech in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, with a litany of catastrophes and suffering: floods in Nepal, heat waves, forests engulfed in flames, rivers running dry, and crop failures caused by drought. "Millions of people are facing hunger," said Radovan, of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "And one thing is clear: The climate crisis is threatening the entire world. No country can tackle it alone." Radovan opened the debate on the federal government's proposed 2027 budget for her ministry with a stark assessment. The budget is set to shrink for the fifth consecutive year, falling from just over €10 billion to just under €9.5 billion ($10.9 billion). In 2022, it stood at nearly €14 billion, meaning that the ministry's budget has been reduced by roughly one-third over the past half decade. How does this sharp decline square with the dramatic picture painted by Germany's development minister? She pointed to a strategy she unveiled in January, when she declared that "development policy will become an even more important pillar of German security, alongside diplomacy and defense." Funding for humanitarian aid stagnates Aid organizations reacted skeptically to this policy shift when it was first announced, and their concerns have deepened in light of the latest funding cuts. "The renewed reductions in funding for international cooperation are further exacerbating an already critical situation," said Michael Herbst of VENRO, the umbrella organization representing around 150 development and humanitarian NGOs. Herbst criticized the stagnant budget for humanitarian aid administered by the German Foreign Office. While it exceeded €3 billion in 2022, it has remained at just €1 billion since 2025. In light of worsening global crises, VENRO is calling for a change of course. "Next year, we will need to invest more in combating hunger because the conflict involving Iran and the dry summer are expected to trigger a sharp decline in agricultural yields," Herbst said, explaining the organization's demand for substantially higher funding. Ten million people left without assistance The impact of the cuts is already clearly visible, according to VENRO. A survey of its member organizations found that the number of funded projects is declining significantly. "Our sample of 34 organizations shows that, among these organizations alone, more than ten million fewer people are being reached with assistance." "And many local partner organizations, which are indispensable to effective development cooperation and humanitarian assistance, are no longer able to operate," Herbst said. He added that the full impact of these far-reaching cuts is unlikely to become apparent for another three to four years. A 'debt brake' exemption for development? The federal government's belt-tightening across virtually all ministries is a consequence of the Zeitenwende announced by 2022 Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Since then, Germany has embarked on a major military buildup, increasing its defense budget year after year, while nearly all other ministries have had to make do with significantly less funding. Herbst, a member of VENRO's executive board, is calling on the Bundestag to exempt both development cooperation and humanitarian assistance from Germany's "debt brake." "After all, exceptions have already been made for the modernization of the Bundeswehr and for military aid to Ukraine," he said. Herbst said an exemption would enable Germany to once again assume greater responsibility on the international stage. Less money, less impact? Jamila Schäfer, a member of parliament from the opposition Green Party, made a similar argument during the Bundestag debate on the Development Ministry's budget. Climate action and development cooperation, she argued, are not acts of charity but are firmly in Germany's own interest. "Germany must invest in its defense capabilities, but security is not created through investments in the defense budget alone," Schäfer said. "Those who strengthen military security while cutting support for international stability have a blind spot in their security policy." Nicolas Zippelius, a lawmaker from the governing center-right conservative alliance, the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), sees the ongoing cuts to development spending differently. In his view, every ministry must contribute to consolidating the federal budget. "Less money does not necessarily mean a smaller impact. Instead, it should encourage us to focus more clearly on priorities and critically review existing structures." Zippelius dismisses demands to exempt the Development Ministry from Germany's debt brake. "The key question is whether every euro spent is directed to where it can make the greatest difference." The Christian Democrat argues that success in development cooperation, as in other areas of policy, should be judged not by the size of the budget but by the impact it achieves. The case for more prevention Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, who heads the humanitarian and development aid organizationAction Against Hunger, has a very different view. "The cuts planned for the 2027 budget are short-sighted and dangerous. As a result, up to 22.6 million people worldwide could die by 2030," he said in a written statement to DW. Cuts to development cooperation and humanitarian aid are also fiscally short-sighted, Friedrich-Rust said. "Hunger, crises and instability generate long-term costs that far exceed the cost of prevention. Those who cut spending today are merely postponing the bill and ultimately making it much more expensive," he warned. To underscore its concerns, the Action Against Hunger alliance delivered a petition to the leaders of the governing coalition of SPD and CDU/CSU parliamentary groups on the eve of the Bundestag's budget debate. About 100,000 people added their names to the appeal, titled "Don't Balance the Budget at the Expense of Solidarity: Strengthen International Aid!" This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Europe seeks stricter age limits for TikTok, Instagram and Facebook
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.07
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, unveiled a plan aimed at keeping children away from the risks associated with some social media platforms. The initiative seeks to prevent children younger than 13 from accessing platforms such as Facebook, TikTok and Instagram. "What we already have is a consensus that there needs to be a start date for the age children can join social media," von der Leyen said, calling for "age-appropriate restrictions." The measure follows similar proposals introduced in Australia, the United Kingdom, China, India, Turkey, and several European countries, and responds to growing concerns about the impact social media can have on children's mental health. "Today, our children are interacting with some of the most sophisticated technologies ever created, and they were not designed with their well-being and development in mind," von der Leyen said at a press conference. The proposed reform to the EU Kids Act "will establish clear boundaries in the digital world, just as we do every day in the real world," she added. Do European laws contradict each other? The non-profit organization CCIA Europe, which represents major technology companies in Europe, including Google and Meta, warned about potential privacy risks stemming from the proposal and pointed to "conflicting requirements" under other European Union laws. "Collecting age information, identity credentials, and data linking children to their parents or guardians on this scale would undoubtedly create an attractive target for cybercriminals," said CCIA Europe Director Daniel Friedlaender. "The Kids Act creates legal overlap and regulatory duplication that ultimately weakens protections for children and consumers," he added. More parental control and stricter regulations Von der Leyen's proposal would give parents greater control over the accounts of young people aged 13 to 15. The initiative will be debated among EU member states and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law. Social media accounts, video streaming services, online video games, and chatbots aimed at users under 18 would be subject to a set of stricter regulations. These include banning features considered addictive, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay content. The proposal would also restrict algorithm-driven recommendations, personalized profiling, reward-based engagement mechanisms, and unsolicited contact from strangers. Another demand from the European Parliament is that platforms be required to implement child-safe designs and algorithms, while also providing easy-to-use parental controls. In addition, major technology companies would have to strengthen their age-verification systems for anyone seeking to open an account. Companies that fail to comply could face fines of up to 6% of their global annual revenue. They would also be required to dedicate greater resources to content supervision and moderation. item.title: Saudi Arabia, Houthis exchange blows as conflict escalates
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.03
At least five people were killed in the escalation between the Iran-backed Houthirebel group and the internationally recognized Yemeni government, supported by Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of a "cowardly" strike on Mecca, the holiest city in Islam and the site of the hajj and umrah pilgrimages, this week. The rebel group denied the accusations. Meanwhile, the Houthis claimed Saudi warplanes targeted three telecommunication towers in Taiz in southwestern Yemen. According to the Almisrah TV channel, backed by the Houthis, one civilian was killed in the town of Abs in the northwest, with the channel later reporting that three children were killed by strikes carried out by Yemen's internationally recognized government. In Saudi Arabia, one person was killed by shrapnel from a downed drone in the Mecca area, the country's civil defense agency said. Damage was also caused to buildings and vehicles. This was the first reported death in Saudi Arabia in the current escalation between the two sides. Houthis advance along coast after collapse of truce A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace. As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014. The rebel group has reported dozens of Saudi strikes since its recent offensive to secure control over the coastal areas near the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes, from government hands. The strait's importance has increased since Iran put restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz over the US and Israel's war with Tehran. The conflict in Yemen has forced more than 100,000 people to flee their homes, according to UN figures. item.title: Chancellor Merz seeks CDU support amid far-right AfD surge
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.70
Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Rovaniemi in northern Finland — nearly 1,800 kilometers (about 1,100 miles) north of Berlin — but even that wasn't far enough to escape the unrest brewing in the German capital. Representatives from various countries had gathered there for the European Arctic Summit to discuss natural resources, geopolitics, security and climate change. When asked by journalists about the mood in Berlin, the chancellor said he could understand the heated debate in Germany surrounding him but that the future of Europe was far more urgent. "That's why I'm trying to convince my friends, my political party, and my parliamentary caucus that this is important — much more important than some of the domestic political debates we're having," he said. Merz was referring to the discussions and rumors circulating about whether he is still the right person for the job — not even a year and a half after he took office as German chancellor back in May 2025. That's because public support for the federal government has hit a record low, and the chancellor's party, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), recently suffered a crushing defeat in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. Why is Merz so unpopular? Another heavy defeat looks likely in the state election coming up in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the lead-up to voting on September 20, the chancellor's party is polling at a dramatically low 7%. Failure to clear the 5% hurdle to enter the state parliament even seems possible. Whatever happens, the CDU is likely to record its worst-ever results in a state election. The election earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt was won by the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, in this central German state. Before taking office, Merz promised he would cut support for the AfD "in half." Instead, support for Merz's own party has dropped by half, and political circles in Berlin are asking: Is this Merz's fault? Is it perhaps due to his often abrasive communication style, or his failure to clearly explain important reforms — such as the one regarding the state pension system? Members of the government are speaking openly about the lack of trust in the Merz cabinet. Education Minister Karin Prien (also of the CDU), for example, said on the public broadcaster ARD: "I believe that many people feel that the chancellor — and we in the CDU/CSU as well — lack the necessary empathy. And that has to change." One frequently heard view is that Merz often comes across as lacking restraint. The planned pension reform, for example, would mean difficult cuts for many, but Merz often seems impatient when discussing it, commentators say. Back in July, the chancellor complained publicly that many citizens' attitudes about a "four-day workweek and work-life balance" could jeopardize the country's prosperity. Trade union representatives were outraged that the chancellor had accused Germans of being "lazy." When the microphones and cameras are off, governing officials speak even more bluntly. The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the CDU's junior coalition partner, are also sounding the alarm. "You really get the impression that nerves are a bit frayed in the CDU right now," said SPD Parliamentary Secretary Dirk Wiese on the Welt TV channel. "I can only appeal once again to our coalition partner to really get back on track and work with us to do things better." Two chancellor candidates: Söder and Wüst But the problem remains that even if the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), agree that Merz must step down as chancellor, there is no clear successor. CSU leader Markus Söder, the Bavarian state premier, has been named as a possible candidate. However, he often and readily provokes the CDU and therefore lacks broad support within the party. Another candidate would be Hendrik Wüst, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state. Although he has quite capably led a coalition with the environmentalist Green Party for over four years, he has so far shown little inclination to move to Berlin. And most importantly, Wüst plans to run for reelection next April in North Rhine-Westphalia. Provided there was enough support for a change of leadership in the governing coalition, there would be no major procedural challenges. Following the resignation of the chancellor, a successor is then appointed by parliamentary majority in the Bundestag. However, if the sitting chancellor doesn't voluntarily step down, a "constructive vote of no confidence" is required. In this case, Wüst or Söder would have to openly challenge Merz — a scenario that no one can imagine at the moment. Perhaps for this reason, too, all eight CDU state premiers declared in a joint statement on Wednesday that they still stood behind Merz. The statement reads: "People can trust that we will address their problems. As state premiers, we want to — and will — contribute to this effort together with the chancellor." Germany needs "stability more than ever," the premiers said on Wednesday, calling for unity within the CDU and arguing that rebuilding voters' trust meant "listening and political action, not personnel debates." All eight premiers signed the statement: Daniel Günther of Schleswig-Holstein, Boris Rhein of Hesse, Sven Schulze of Saxony-Anhalt, Kai Wegner of Berlin, Michael Kretschmer of Saxony, Gordon Schnieder of Rhineland-Palatinate, Mario Voigt of Thuringia and Wüst of North Rhine-Westphalia. Pivotal state elections coming up So while there isn't really a clear alternative to Merz, the chancellor also isn't someone who is likely to simply step down. If rumors circulating in political circles in Berlin are to be believed, Merz wants to convene the executive committee of the CDU in Berlin as early as this coming Sunday evening, once the results of the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are in. His plan is to stand in front of this group of 22 leading conservative politicians and pose the question of whether his party is still willing to put its trust in him. Merz's schedule for the coming week illustrates just how seriously he views the situation. The chancellor has canceled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly, an engagement that had been planned well in advance and was treated as a fixed appointment. "Contrary to the original plans, he will not travel to New York, as he is needed in Berlin," government sources have confirmed. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: EU seeks Arctic strategy amid growing power rivalry
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.61
Known as the "Gateway to the Arctic," the Finnish city of Rovaniemi sits directly on the Arctic Circle. Its forests are glowing in autumn colors as European leaders gather here at the invitation of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to discuss a new EU strategy for the Arctic. Climate change and Russia's war against Ukraine have thrust the High North into the center of European attention. "There is a high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic," Orpo said. "Our security environment has changed fundamentally. The Arctic has emerged as a central arena of great power competition." The prime minister added that the Arctic's critical natural resources are also "attracting interest." A changing security environment in the High North The changing security environment was a central theme throughout the summit. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Russia is reopening former Soviet military bases in the region and conducting missile exercises in the High North. "We also see that China is increasingly more interested in the region, so we have to remain vigilant," Kallas said. The leaders gathered at Finland's northernmost air force base, looking up into a cloudless blue sky as Finnish fighter jets took to the air for a demonstration. Security has been placed at the heart of the discussions by Prime Minister Orpo. From Rovaniemi, Finland's Air Force monitors the skies along Europe's Arctic border with Russia ― 24/7. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who attended despite facing significant political pressure at home, described the region as increasingly important to Europe's security: "This region has become a geopolitical hotspot. Russia is building up its military capabilities here and … uses its presence for hybrid activities every day." Merz added that the Arctic is not only a security issue, but also offers major economic opportunities, particularly when it comes to critical raw materials. Confrontation replaces cooperation "From the Putin era onwards, Russia has been developing its military capacities everywhere, but also in the Arctic," said Timo Koivurova of the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland. For years Western countries still continued cooperating with Moscow on scientific research and climate issues. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought that era to an end. Finland and Sweden joined NATO as a direct consequence of the war. Finland's 1,340-kilometer (833-mile) border with Russia is now also a NATO border, fundamentally changing the security landscape in northern Europe. The European Commission plans to update its 2021 Arctic Strategy as early as October 2026. The summit's joint declaration calls for greater investment in military mobility, cross-border connectivity and critical infrastructure in the EU's northernmost regions, including transport links, digital networks and satellite technologies. Koivurova said that Russia's current focus on Ukraine and that war takes its military capacities. "But obviously when that war is over, and someday it will be over, there will be a lot of investments from Russia, very likely also in the northern regions, because they are so important for its overall security," Koivurova told DW. The United States as an additional stress factor The Arctic is also being affected by tensions among Western partners, Koivurova said. In particular, he argued that US President Donald Trump's proposals regarding Canada and Greenland have strained cooperation among Arctic allies. "Trump's proposal to have Canada as the 51st state of the United States, or the purchase of Greenland, these are really major problems for the cooperative relations between the western Arctic states," Koivurova said. "That is a kind of additional stress factor for Arctic governance cooperation." Veteran Arctic observer Markku Heikkilä believes the region is increasingly divided. "In my opinion, [the] Arctic is now slowly dividing into three parts," Heikkilä told DW. He said Russia forms one bloc, while countries such as EU member states, Norway, Iceland and Canada continue to defend a rules-based international order, climate action and Indigenous rights. "Officially the position of the USA is now very much different from what it used to be," said Heikkilä. Climate change is transforming the Arctic At the same time, climate change is reshaping the Arctic faster than any other region on Earth. Scientists expect the central Arctic Ocean to become largely ice-free during summer sometime around 2040 and 2050. As sea ice retreats, the region is gaining strategic importance with new shipping routes and significantly shortening distances between major trading centers, creating new economic and geopolitical opportunities, says Koivurova. Yet climate policy has become another source of disagreement between the United States and many of its Arctic partners. "Climate change is, of course, a hugely important thing in the Arctic. It's warming four times the rate as compared to the global average. So everything we do in the Arctic nowadays, one way or the other, is related to climate change," Koivurova said. He added that the Trump administration's approach has had a significant impact on international cooperation, including within the Arctic Council: "The US is torpedoing any mention of climate change at the moment. So that was certainly a big, big change." Orpo: 'We should strengthen Arctic resilience' At the close of the summit, Prime Minister Orpo called for greater investment to strengthen the region's resilience. "We should strengthen Arctic resilience by strategic investments in Arctic infrastructure, dual use transport networks, critical raw materials, icebreaking and technological innovation," Orpo said. Rovaniemi is known worldwide as the hometown of Santa Claus. Not far from the "Arktikum" museum and science center where the leaders met lies "Santa Claus Village." It's home to the official Santa Claus Post Office, which remains open year-round. Visitors can also meet Santa himself. Whether any of the summit participants paid him a visit ― and if so, what they wished for ― remains unknown. Edited by: Carla Bleiker

item.title: Nigeria: At least 37 suspected illegal miners die in custody
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.56
At least 37 people believed to be illegal miners died Thursday while in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps (NSCDC), according to the governor of Nigeria's north-central Niger State. "This morning we woke up to the news that about 37 persons died in the custody of the civil defense here in Minna," Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago told reporters in the state's capital. He called the incident "sad" and "tragic," adding that a committee of inquiry into the deaths had been established and was already working. The governor declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for the January elections. The police in Niger State announced that they have launched an investigation and urged relatives of the victims to come forward with any helpful information. What do we know about the incident? The suspects have been detained since the security agency made arrests on Tuesday and Wednesday due to suspicions of illegal mining in the state, said Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, head of the NSCDC in Niger, in a statement on Thursday. Aniviye said that although the agency suspects the detainees died of disease, their bodies were sent to a local hospital for a medical examination to determine the cause of death. He did not specify the type of disease. However, according to the intelligence report, "preliminary information suggests the fatalities may have resulted from overcrowding and inadequate ventilation within a detention facility." A 40-second video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men, most of whom appeared to be teenagers. Volunteers wearing gloves stood over the bodies, while veiled women tried to identify their relatives. Survivors describe a lack of ventilation Dauda Shehu, one of the survivors, told the Associated Press that 65 detainees were packed into a poorly ventilated cell. "We were jampacked and there was no ventilation for us to breathe well," he said. "All of a sudden, we realized that we could not breathe and we started scrambling to get fresh air," Shehu added. The detainees tried to get the guards' attention by banging on the cell door, he explained. Spanning more than twice the area of Belgium, Niger State is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most of whom are lured by the hope of striking gold. According to officials and experts, the scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger State is also fueling violence by criminal gangs known locally as bandits. These gangs tax miners and demand a cut of the extracted ore in exchange for access to the pits. Edited by: Sean Sinico Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
