item.title: What’s the Matter With Eastern Germany?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.96
What’s the Matter With Eastern Germany? German far-right populism traces back to reunification—but historians disagree about why. There’s a widespread consensus in Germany that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is a xenophobic far-right party that threatens the republic’s postwar political order. But there’s no accord on remedies—and, relatedly, no agreement about the sources of the scourge. What seems clear is that the AfD’s variety of national populism is most heavily anchored in eastern Germany and traces back to the country’s Cold War division, the terms of its eventual unification, and East-West relations since 1990. But that surface-level agreement about recent history masks deeper disagreements about what exactly happened during those periods. There’s a widespread consensus in Germany that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is a xenophobic far-right party that threatens the republic’s postwar political order. But there’s no accord on remedies—and, relatedly, no agreement about the sources of the scourge. What seems clear is that the AfD’s variety of national populism is most heavily anchored in eastern Germany and traces back to the country’s Cold War division, the terms of its eventual unification, and East-West relations since 1990. But that surface-level agreement about recent history masks deeper disagreements about what exactly happened during those periods. The AfD is not solely an eastern German phenomenon: Parties like it exist across the European Union, in the United Kingdom, and in the United States, too. In western Germany, the AfD breaks into double digits everywhere and even tops 20 percent in places. But its popularity is twice as high across eastern Germany—where polled rates of xenophobic sentiment are also much higher. The record result of 44 percent in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections on Sept. 6 is conceivable only in an eastern state, at least for now. One school of German historians explains the eastern mentality through the prism of the German Democratic Republic’s (GDR) fundamentally totalitarian character. Its clearest proponent is Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk, a historian affiliated with the Stasi Records Archive, the repository of the GDR’s secret police files. Kowalczuk hails from a GDR family that was closely tied to the regime, a story he tells in his book Freiheitsschock (Freedom Shock), but broke with his family and cast off the system’s Marxist-Leninist straitjacket, which cost him the opportunity to attend university. (After unification, he studied history at Humboldt University.) At 22, he joined the countrywide demonstrations that eventually chased out GDR hardliners and caused the Berlin Wall to fall. Kowalczuk emphasizes the all-encompassing totality of a state that dictated every facet of life to its subjects: “from cradle to grave,” indoctrinating and controlling through schools, party, mass organizations, and the workplace. Most historians who argue along Kowalczuk’s lines hold that the Stasi itself, through informant networks and an all-knowing, all-powerful apparatus, kept the GDR’s population of 16 million in line. Kowalczuk, however, argues that the Stasi itself was not as powerful as claimed or thought (or as portrayed in The Lives of Others): Much of its power of intimidation stemmed from its reputation, not its actual reach. In other words, eastern Germans, argues Kowalczuk, could have acted more independently and even defiantly had they had the gumption—but they didn’t. Kowalczuk argues that East Germans passively allowed themselves to be subjugated, browbeaten, restricted, and instructed by the regime. They were obedient pupils internalizing its narrow-minded, racist, authoritarian character and reproducing it in families, schools, and society. He casts eastern Germans essentially as sheep who relinquished freedom in exchange for certainty and security. In his view, the so-called peaceful revolution of 1989 wasn’t instigated by these cowed masses but by a tiny minority of dissidents and rebels—like himself. The public took to the streets only once the regime was on the run, and then portrayed themselves as freedom fighters—and victims. The newly liberated East Germans had no conception of an alternative state or society beyond that which then-West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the “reunification chancellor,” dangled before their eyes. Today’s eastern Germans, Kowalczuk says—even those born in a unified Germany—have undertaken too little to emancipate themselves from the GDR’s totalitarian mindset. They refuse to take responsibility for their own condition, demand the state provide for them, and express the same intolerance toward other cultures that the regime once did. The uncertainties that freedom presents are so unnerving that they retreat into nostalgia for the GDR—beyond even that in Goodbye, Lenin!—that idealizes its old ties to the Soviet Union and sympathizes with a dictator as ruthless as Vladimir Putin. Kowalczuk’s most direct foil is Katja Hoyer, also a GDR-born historian, though she was only 4 years old when the peaceful revolution broke out. She’s known to English-language readers through her UK bestseller Beyond the Wall: East Germany, 1949 – 1990, which argues that life in the GDR was more textured than Kowalczuk acknowledges. East Germans lived and loved, had birthday parties and weddings, and enjoyed vacations and families. They weren’t passive, she argues, despite the formidable security apparatus. The GDR’s film industry—during periods of liberalization—even produced quality films like the 1973 cult classic Die Legende von Paul und Paula (The Legend of Paul and Paula). Hoyer also credits GDR socialism with genuine achievements, such as women’s rights, affordable housing, and hands-on workplace participation. If unglamorous, just about everyone had a two-room apartment and, of course, a job. Rents were subsidized, healthcare free, and there was childcare for all families. Hoyer treats the relative material equality of the self-described “workers’ and farmers’ state” as a humane alternative to capitalism’s wealth gaps. “Many East Germans were proud of their achievements as social mobility provided unprecedented opportunities for the working classes,” she argues. Although Beyond the Wall stops in 1990, elsewhere Hoyer argues that eastern Germans’ lives and achievements were dismissed in the united Germany as worthless “ballast.” West German condescension and the “sink or swim” into which eastern Germans were thrown in the 1990s caused resentment to fester, and snowball, and be passed on to subsequent generations. The problem today in Germany’s eastern states, she argues, isn’t that citizens are undemocratic but that the system is less democratic than they had expected. Materially, the easterners lag behind their western brethren not least because they had no assets when communism collapsed. She has sympathy for the hardships that economic union imposed. Seen this way, the AfD vote is explicable. This party alone avoids demonizing the GDR, thus offering eastern Germans respect that none of the other parties do. The AfD may be German, Hoyer argues, but versions of it exist everywhere in Europe, including England, where she currently works. Eastern Germans’ “behaviors and characteristics have lazily been written off as a deviation from the west German norm, fostering a defiant us-against-them mentality,” she argued in 2024 in the Guardian. “This east German identity, combined with the feeling of being othered and marginalised, is a powerful thing for the AFD to exploit.” As for the racism and xenophobia, she attributes them to economic anxiety and condescension. The way to win back the easterners is to take their concerns seriously, including migration, and treat them with respect. A third prominent commentator is Dirk Oschmann, a literature professor at Leipzig University. His take in Der Osten: eine westdeutsche Erfindung (The East: A West German Invention), a 2023 work widely discussed in Germany, is close to Hoyer’s but not identical. He contends that the western Germans’ derogatory labeling of easterners as lazy, dim-witted, bigoted complaining losers is a means to deflect legitimate criticism that the West itself flubbed unification. He argues that the lock-stock-and-barrel incorporation of eastern Germany into the Federal Republic constituted a one-sided takeover. There was, for example, no constitutional convention to create the unified Germany anew. East Germany’s economy was put on equal footing with West Germany’s overnight, causing it to implode—while western companies swooped into pick up the business. The East’s factories and firms were sold off to Western buyers, who made out like bandits. West German elites stepped into leadership posts across the East: in universities, police forces, hospitals—just about everywhere. Oschmann considers Kowalczuk a proponent of this tendency by tracing everything back to the GDR itself, rather than the humiliation of unification and the travails of decades since. He explains the AfD and the power of the migration issue much as Hoyer does: as a response to grievances and disrespect. As for the East’s cultural racism, he admits its presence but calls the West’s pejorative treatment of the East a form of xenophobia or “othering.” This surfeit of analysis begs the question of whether any response from the mainstream German parties can win AfD voters to their side. Certainly, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz thinks so. His remedy is to double down on restricting migration, the top reason for AfD voting. This was Merz’s answer before the Saxony-Anhalt vote and, while asylum applications have fallen by nearly half under Merz, there’s been no political payoff. Rather than vote for the copy act, 44 percent of Saxony-Anhalt’s voters cast their ballots for the original, the AfD, whose jingoism Merz chases after, while the CDU was rewarded with less than half of its previous vote share. The Social Democrats think better social safety nets will do the trick, even though AfD voters are not poor. Germany’s political establishment is clueless how to handle the AfD’s surge—and the country’s historians, sadly, offer no concrete answers either. Paul Hockenos is a Berlin-based journalist. His recent book is Berlin Calling: A Story of Anarchy, Music, the Wall, and the Birth of the New Berlin. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: By Nearly Every Metric, the U.S. Is Losing the Iran War
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.07
By Nearly Every Metric, the U.S. Is Losing the Iran War “It’s irrefutable that the U.S. failed in its main strategic goals,” one expert said. In early March, U.S. President Donald Trump said that the United States had already “won” the war against Iran but still had to “finish the job.” Months later, as fighting escalates across the region and diplomacy is stalled, the “job” remains unfinished with no end in sight. Trump on Wednesday said that “hopefully we are toward the end of the war” and suggested that Iran wants to make a deal. But that optimism is belied by what’s happening on the ground—and there’s little evidence that Tehran is eager for an agreement. In early March, U.S. President Donald Trump said that the United States had already “won” the war against Iran but still had to “finish the job.” Months later, as fighting escalates across the region and diplomacy is stalled, the “job” remains unfinished with no end in sight. Trump on Wednesday said that “hopefully we are toward the end of the war” and suggested that Iran wants to make a deal. But that optimism is belied by what’s happening on the ground—and there’s little evidence that Tehran is eager for an agreement. The United States has had military successes in the war, but, overall, the conflict has been a strategic disaster for Washington. The fighting has exposed serious vulnerabilities for the U.S. military and left its forces spread thin, cost the United States an estimated $38.1 billion so far, and caused a global energy crisis. The war is extremely unpopular with American voters, and a growing number of Republicans in Congress are voting in favor of ending the conflict; one GOP congressman has even moved to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war. But for all of those costs, the United States has achieved very little in Iran—and in some cases, things have gotten worse. By nearly every metric—from Iran’s ability to project power in the region through its proxies, to its military capabilities, to the strength of its regime, to the status of its nuclear program—the United States is losing the war. What’s more, Tehran has now proved that it can shut down the Strait of Hormuz long term, an ability it long boasted of having but had never actually demonstrated. “If you wind the clock back to February and take a look at what the U.S. stated it was trying to do, it’s irrefutable that the U.S. failed in its main strategic goals,” Gregory Brew, an Iran expert and senior analyst at Eurasia Group, told Foreign Policy. Proxies When Trump announced the onset of major combat operations against Iran in late February, he said that the United States was going to ensure that “terrorist proxies can no longer destabilize the region or the world and attack our forces.” Similarly, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine in early March said that the United States was aiming to dismantle “Iran’s ability to project power outside of its borders, both today and in the future.” In a primetime speech to the nation a month into the war, Trump also said the United States was “systematically dismantling the [Iranian] regime’s ability to threaten America or project power outside of their borders.” But there’s no evidence to suggest that the United States has accomplished this. The fact that the conflict has for months been centered on a fight for control of the Strait of Hormuz—a waterway that was open when the war began—is indicative of Tehran’s enduring capacity to influence the course of events both in the Middle East and wider world (more on that below). Tehran’s proxies also remain a major threat months into the war and are increasingly contributing to both regional chaos and rising oil prices. The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen made major territorial gains along the country’s Red Sea coast this month, including seizing the port city of Mocha and strategic islands like Perim, in a blistering offensive against Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. As a result, the group has taken effective control over another critical waterway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and separates the Arabian Peninsula from Africa. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait was already a key shipping lane before the war but became even more important amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran and the Houthis for months warned that the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could be closed if the United States continued the war, and they are now in a position to make good on that threat. Meanwhile, the Houthis and Saudi Arabia are exchanging fire, reigniting long-running tensions tied to a civil war that began in 2014 but were largely on pause following a 2022 truce. There are now growing concerns that Yemen is on the verge of returning to full-blown civil war. Saudi Arabia also temporarily shut down its 750-mile East-West oil pipeline last week after it was damaged in a drone attack that Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed militants in Iraq, and it’s unclear when it will be operational again. The pipeline transports crude oil from the kingdom’s east to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, and its temporary closure impacts roughly 4 percent of the world’s oil supply. It’s true that other Iranian proxies like Hamas and Hezbollah—long considered Tehran’s most powerful ally in the region—are now far weaker than they were a few years ago, but this is almost entirely due to Israeli actions in Gaza and Lebanon. Ballistic missiles and drones The Trump administration also launched the war with the objective of destroying Iran’s ballistic missile and drone capabilities. In April, Hegseth said Iran’s missile program was functionally destroyed and that the country could “no longer build missiles.” Trump has also claimed that Iran’s military has been “totally destroyed.” Iran’s military has certainly been significantly affected by the war. A number of top Iranian military and intelligence leaders have been killed since the bombs started falling, its industrial capacity has been diminished, and its conventional navy has largely been destroyed. But Tehran’s continued ability to launch attacks on targets across the region with both missiles and drones shows that this goal remains elusive and that the Trump administration has greatly embellished its military successes. Intelligence assessments also contradict the Trump administration’s public claims about the extent to which Iran’s military has been degraded. Iran has reportedly resumed ballistic missile production in underground facilities, even after thousands of U.S. strikes targeted its missile facilities and launch sites in the early days of the war. It was also always going to be difficult to completely destroy Iran’s drone capability given how cheap and easy they are to produce. Regime change While the Trump administration has fluctuated on whether bringing down the Iranian regime is a central objective, when the war began it was clear that toppling Iran’s leadership was among the White House’s key goals. “To the great proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” Trump said on Feb. 28. “When we are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take. This will be probably your only chance for generations.” Though top Iranian leaders, including former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, have been killed, the regime remains very much intact and, in many ways, has only calcified. “Insofar as regime change was a goal, U.S. action has been almost entirely counterproductive. The regime is now more entrenched. It is more confident of its position inside Iran. It is more emboldened. It’s dominated now by military security leadership that, while pragmatic, are almost uniformly hostile toward the West and not interested in any kind of broader accommodation with the U.S. or the West in general,” Brew said. Nuclear program More than any other issue, Trump has repeatedly returned to Iran’s nuclear program as the primary objective of the war. The president has also misleadingly claimed that the United States “obliterated” Iran’s program, even as he justifies continuing the war for the sake of preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. There’s no doubt that U.S. strikes have set Iran’s nuclear program back by destroying infrastructure and killing important figures within Iran (including top scientists), but the country still has a roughly 440-kilogram (970 pounds) stockpile of highly enriched uranium (HEU). Experts have repeatedly emphasized that as long as Iran has access to this stockpile—the precise location of which remains unknown—its nuclear program remains a threat and cannot be considered neutralized. International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director-General Rafael Grossi this week lamented that the agency’s oversight of Iran’s nuclear program “deteriorated” this year. “We have not conducted any in-field verification activities in Iran for more than six months,” Grossi said, while emphasizing that it’s been “well over a year” since the IAEA “lost continuity of knowledge” regarding Iran’s uranium stockpile. “The Agency’s lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern and needs to be addressed with the utmost urgency,” Grossi said. Trump has flip-flopped on whether the United States needs to retrieve the country’s HEU stockpile—suggesting it’s buried under rubble and inaccessible due to previous U.S. strikes. “We will get it. We don’t need it, we don’t want it. We’ll probably destroy it after we get it, but we’re not going to let them have it,” Trump said in May. Satellite imagery has also shown a “surge” in construction activity at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site, in 2026, according to a recent analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Last week, Trump suggested the United States could take action based on the reports of construction activity at Pickaxe Mountain. “We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe,” Trump said. “I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard.” Despite such rhetoric, the Trump administration’s actions increasingly indicate that Iran’s nuclear program has been bumped down the White House’s list of priorities. Amid the lack of progress on the nuclear issue and the failure to achieve its initial goals in the war more broadly, the Trump administration has shifted its attention to other objectives. The administration has moved to strangle Iran economically, via both a naval blockade and a financial campaign—dubbed Operation Economic Outcast—to further isolate Tehran via sanctions and other actions. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said as he announced the effort in late August. But Iran’s leadership has withstood economic pressure from the United States for decades, raising doubts as to whether this approach will actually move the needle and see Tehran make concessions in any future talks. Control of Hormuz The war is now fundamentally a fight over oil and shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz. While around 4 million to 5 million barrels of oil were flowing through the strait daily in early August, that number is now approaching around 10 million, Brew said. This is positive for the United States and also comes as its naval blockade appears to be working given Iranian oil exports have ground to a halt. But traffic through the strait is roughly a fifth of what was seen before the war, Brew said, underscoring that the situation is also being “managed through a pretty considerable outlay of resources.” The process involves the U.S. Navy and air assets providing defense for tankers moving through the strait in small convoys. This system has steadily increased the flow of oil through the strait over the last month, and while it’s helping to delay a “general crisis” in energy markets, Brew said, it’s “not removing the risk.” The price of Brent crude—the global benchmark for oil—sat around $104 on Thursday. Just before the war began in February, the price of Brent crude was roughly $72 a barrel. In response to a request for comment on whether Trump believes the war will end on a positive note for the United States, a White House official on background told Foreign Policy that “Iran is calling constantly and is desperate for a deal,” but the president is “only open to making a good deal with Iran, whereby they permanently renounce their desire for a nuclear weapon.” The official also said that while Trump is open to talks under the “right circumstances,” he has “no need to negotiate with the Iranians.” “Unlike previous presidents, President Trump will not be played by the Iranian regime. The President is satisfied letting the inevitable Iranian collapse play out,” the official said. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: AI Is Changing the Rules of Entrepreneurship
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.23
Summary. Today, a single individual enabled by AI can—at very low cost—perform many activities needed to establish a startup quickly and in parallel: generating product ideas, simulating Almost two decades ago, the entrepreneur and author Eric Ries launched a methodology for the “lean startup.” In this approach, a new business could be launched with just capital, a minimum viable product, a team, extensive discussions with potential customers, and a process of repeated pivoting as the startup scaled. The lean startup approach combined Toyota’s lean manufacturing method with Stanford professor Steve Blank’s approaches to customer development. Because founders typically had few resources at their disposal, the lean approach took hold.

item.title: What It Takes to Make Progress When the Future Feels Out of Control
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.13
Share Podcast What It Takes to Make Progress When the Future Feels Out of Control A conversation with psychologist Martin Seligman on the power of agency in building a positive work culture. When the future feels increasingly out of our control, how can leaders and organizations make progress? University of Pennsylvania psychologist Martin Seligman, a pioneer in the study of optimism, resilience, and human flourishing, argues that the answer is agency: the belief that we can influence outcomes and create positive change. He defines agency as a combination of three capabilities: efficacy—the belief that you can achieve a goal now; optimism—the belief that you can achieve it in the future; and imagination—the ability to envision possibilities that don’t yet exist. And he explains how leaders can cultivate these qualities in themselves and their organizations, how managers can help employees overcome catastrophizing, and what AI can—and can’t—do when it comes to one of the most important human capabilities: imagination. Seligman is the author of Agency: The Psychological History of Human Progress. ADI IGNATIUS: I’m Adi Ignatius. ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard, and this is the HBR IdeaCast. ADI IGNATIUS: So, Alison, here’s my question for you today. What does it take to make progress when the future feels out of control? ALISON BEARD: So, I think the psychologist that I’ve talked to over the years would say when you really have no influence on external factors, you’ve got to change your own mindset and behaviors. ADI IGNATIUS: Yeah, I think that’s exactly right. It is a simple idea. It is not at all simple to execute, and it’s actually an essential part of the argument that today’s guest is making. Martin Seligman is a renowned professor of psychology at the University of Pennsylvania, and after decades of studying optimism, resilience, and human flourishing, he has set his sights on agency, on how we can have more of it to achieve positive outcomes. He defines agency as being made up of three things, efficacy, the belief that you can achieve a goal now, optimism, the belief that you can achieve it in the future, and imagination, the ability to envision possibilities that don’t yet exist. ALISON BEARD: Yeah, all of those sound like hallmarks of any successful business leader I can think of, but I’d love to hear more about how people and organizations can cultivate them. ADI IGNATIUS: All right. Well, stay tuned. We will hear advice from Seligman on how to do just that. Plus, what’s happening to Agency as AI gets more integrated into the world. He’s the author of a new book, Agency: The Psychological History of Human Progress. Here’s our conversation. So, I love the ideas you’re exploring in the book about agency, about progress. I also want to talk about how businesses and individuals can think about and apply these findings, but let’s start with agency. MARTY SELIGMAN: Agency is a psychological state that has three components. It’s overall the belief that you can do it. The first component is efficacy, and that’s the belief that you can achieve a specific goal in the here and now. The second component is optimism, and that’s the belief that you can achieve that goal in the far future. And the third is imagination. That’s the range of goals that you can achieve in the future. Efficacy works by trying. If you believe you can do it, you try. Optimism works by persistence and maintenance. If you believe you can do it in the far future, you overcome obstacles and do it. And imagination works by innovation. The notion of agency says that when individual human agency is high, that’s when you get progress. ADI IGNATIUS: So, if you define agency as you did, as efficacy, optimism and imagination, if you were advising a CEO, which of those three do you think organizations are most deficient in? MARTY SELIGMAN: Let me give you the background to my answer here, and indeed I’ll say the way in which I would and in fact do advise CEOs. In the middle of the Iraq War, the chief of staff of the Army, George Casey, called me to the Pentagon and basically said, “Post-traumatic stress disorder, suicide, panic, divorce, drug abuse. What does positive psychology say about that?” And my answer to that was we should move the entire distribution of soldiers from post-traumatic stress disorder in the direction of post-traumatic growth. So, I became the chief civilian in comprehensive soldier fitness, and that led me to a study of success versus failure in the army. The army is not only a bigger corporation than Walmart, but it’s got 130 different job descriptions. So, on day one, everyone in the army takes a hundred item questionnaire that we designed about psychological strengths and weaknesses. 900,000 people, we follow them for five years, and the army has two medals that it gives relevant to your question about advising a CEO. The first is exemplary work and the second is heroism. In five years, 12% of a population, 12% of the army wins those medals. So, the question is, can you predict it from day one statistically? And the answer is robustly yes. There are three variables that predict exemplary work. The first is high optimism, the second is high positive emotion, and the third is low negative emotion, not being a complainer. Now, that tells essentially CEO, hire happy people, but CEO realistically doesn’t have the freedom to only hire happy people. And then the second piece of advice is we now know quite a bit about interventions that build efficacy, optimism, and imagination. So, hire happy people and train, teach your pessimists the techniques of optimism. So, we had, again, this is not a sample. We have the entire army here, 75,000 people in five years deployed to Iraq or Afghanistan. 3,500 of them, about 5% are diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder. There are two predictors of post-traumatic stress disorder. One we already knew, and that was how awful is the combat? But most interestingly, it’s the catastrophizers, the people who believe when bad events occur, everything unravels, are more than twice as likely to come down with PTSD. So, there are two lessons here for the CEO, hire happy people and train unhappy people about wellbeing. And secondly, avoid catastrophizers. ADI IGNATIUS: So, I mean, this has profound implications. How do leaders encourage optimism without creating a culture of unrealistic confidence or wishful thinking that is also uncalled for? MARTY SELIGMAN: Superficial optimism, mouthing the words doesn’t work. It’s no good for a CEO to get in there and say, “We’re going to crush them. Everything’s going to work out.” So, the question is, how can you learn non-shallow optimism? I’m a pessimist, a depressive by birth, and I’ve had to develop a lot of the techniques myself and use them. And indeed, one of the most effective techniques which produces a real optimism is disputation. So, Adi, I woke up at 4:00 AM, and I said to myself, “Oh my God, HBR, they’re right at the edge of leadership and corporations. I’m 84 years old. I live in the past. I’m over the hill. I can’t possibly do an HBR interview.” That’s actually what I said to myself at 4:00 in the morning. And indeed, as a pessimist and a depressive, the automatic thoughts never go away, but I have become a very good arguer against them. I said, “Hey, wait a minute. I did two interviews last week and they went splendidly” Now, importantly, argument against catastrophic thinking has to be realistic. You have to treat these thoughts, not as gospel, but as something that’s being said to you by a person whose mission in life was to make you miserable, who’s a rival for your job, and your job is to dispute it realistically. ADI IGNATIUS: So, if you were in charge of, let’s say, redesigning a corporation specifically to maximize the kind of human agency that can lead to progress, what would you change? How would you think about this organizationally? MARTY SELIGMAN: Hire happy people, one. Take your unhappy people and teach them techniques like disputation and decastrophization. Avoid complainers. Now, there’s a lot more that I think a CEO can do, and one of them has to do with imagination and abduction. I think it’s the imaginative corporation that’s going to innovate more. And I work on imagination and it’s a difficult thing. So, like almost everyone you’ve probably interviewed, I’ve been doing AI almost full-time for the last couple of years. Right at the beginning of ChatGPT, one of my former graduate student who’s a professor in Beijing emailed me and said, “Hey, Marty, we’ve got the same problems of depression, anxiety, suicide in China that you do in America, but we don’t have enough therapists or coaches to go around, so we’ve created a virtual Seligman. We fed it with all of your books and speeches. Try it out.” You can ask for advice, like my boss is a micromanager, and you get my voice in either Mandarin or in English giving you advice. The advice is generally very good, but for our purposes, I’ve been interested in the question of hallucinations and its relationship to creativity and imagination. So, I’ve now looked at a thousand of the Ask Martin responses, and it only hallucinated once. Here’s what it led to. I went back to Claude and I said, “Okay, are you a coherence machine or a correspondence machine?” The two theories of truth: correspondence theory that P is true if P obtains in the world, cat is on the mat is true if the cat is on the mat. Coherence is not about reality, it’s about what you already believe.” And Claude said, “Marty, I’m a coherence machine. Well, I don’t have sensors, eyes, ears, hands. Everything you hear from me is an expansion and coherent with what I already believe.” So, I said, “What are the 20 greatest accomplishments in human science? How many of those could you have done on your own?” “Well, I could have done seven. I would’ve done plate tectonics, it just fits South America to Africa. I could have done Mendelian genetics, Algebra. I could have done Big Bang. It’s a mathematication of explosions over time.” “Which couldn’t you have done?” “Well, I couldn’t have done Darwin and I couldn’t have done Einstein. I don’t do abduction. I don’t make leaps to the best explanation possible.” So, I’ve become very interested in the teaching of abduction, which I think is uniquely human and the machines cannot by their very design being coherence machines do it. We need more imagination at the cutting edge of a corporation, and we need to come to understand and train the notion of taking leaps beyond the evidence, the notion of abduction. And that’s something I’m intimately involved in now, trying to teach people to become better leapers of explanations. I think a lot of success has to do with leaping beyond the evidence. ADI IGNATIUS: I want to get back to the question of how you set up organizations that can achieve the right level of agency. This is a question that companies face all the time. To what extent do you empower people? You talked about hiring the right people and trying to make them less pessimistic, teach them to be less pessimistic and to see possibilities. But there are also some basic questions about what is the right level of agency to… People look to leaders to provide answers, but it may be that a leader’s most important job is really to make other people feel they could affect outcomes, that they have that kind of agency. So how do you think about that interplay between the agency of the leader versus empowering people at all levels to have that same kind of agency? At some level, it’s the paradox of management. MARTY SELIGMAN: There are techniques beyond empowerment that make people better at agency. So, I want to take catastrophization. So, remember I said in our study of 75,000 soldiers deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan, it was the catastrophizers who come down with PTSD. Now, catastrophization is a paralyzer. It not only feels bad, but it makes you helpless and paralyzes you and undermines imagination, optimism, and efficacy. Here’s the technique. It’s called put it in perspective. Close your eyes for a moment, Adi, if you would. It’s noon on Friday and you get an email from your boss that says, “Come see me at 4:00.” Now, what do you think? Well, almost everyone catastrophizes. ADI IGNATIUS: This is bad. MARTY SELIGMAN: But some are extreme catastrophizers. So, here’s what we do systematically: say, “Okay, what’s the very worst that can happen at 4:00?” “Well, she read my memo on the advertising campaign. She hates it and I’m going to be fired. Okay. What’s the very best that could happen at 4:00?” “Well, she read my memo, she loves it, and I’m getting a raise. ” Okay. “What’s the most likely thing that’s going to happen at 4:00?” “Well, she read my memo. She liked a lot of it, but she thought the budget was over the top.” Okay, what can you do to plan for the most likely scenario?” “Well, I’m going to spend the next three hours going over the budget. I’m going to try to justify the really expensive parts and I’m going to cut the fat in preparation.” Now, we find that when we teach people, put it in perspective, they become significantly less catastrophizing. And so, this is one of several techniques, realistic techniques that CEOs and managers can use beyond urging people to be more optimistic and more imaginative. I think the words of urging are fine, and I think people very often imitate the optimism of their managers, but I think you want to teach the skills underlying efficacy, optimism, and imagination, and one of them is decatastrophization. ADI IGNATIUS: I have to ask about this particular period in time right now. I mean, everybody seems to refer to this period, certainly in the business world as an era of uncertainty, that we’re buffeted by forces we cannot control, whether it’s AI, geopolitics, economic uncertainty, climate change. We have this consensus, right or wrong, that things have never been this out of control, that we’ve never had less agency as leaders, as individuals. What do you think about that? Does this period of an unusual break from the norms we’ve been used to for 50 years, say, require extra levels of thinking about how to get people out of this sense that they are passive victims of forces they can’t control and into a stage of more agency and being able to think again about creating progress? MARTY SELIGMAN: Well, I think this really is a period of uncertainty, and I don’t know any techniques for denying that, but there are some verities here that I guess are general purpose tools against uncertainty. So let me take one very important one that I’ve been involved in, and it’s the relationship of company wellbeing to productivity in times of uncertainty. In the last 20 years, I find myself occasionally with CEOs and CFOs boosting the idea that workers under you should be happy, should be positive, and that positive psychology is a good thing to have in your company. And then the CFO will say something after five minutes like, “Is it profitable?” And up until about a year and a half ago, I honestly had to say there are about five studies in literature of profitability and the happiness of workers, and they go in the direction of the happier the company, the more the… but none of them meet my scientific standards. So, I basically, to be honest, the answer was, “I didn’t know.” Along comes Jan-Emmanuel De Neve about a year and a half ago, a professor at Oxford, and what he’s done is taken 1,600 American companies that employ, I think, 15 million people. And the company takes four wellbeing questions at the outset, the employees, one is how happy are you at work? How satisfied are you with your job? How much purpose and meaning does your job have, and how stressed are you at work? And so, they look at those four questions, they quantify the companies. Then importantly, through this period of uncertainty, they come back nine months later and ask stock market price, profitability, return on investment, and there’s a linear relationship between how happy the company is on those four questions at time one and profitability and stock market price at time two. And so, there’s a verity here, Adi, that’s important, which I wasn’t able to say a year and a half ago that in the face of uncertainty, one thing I think we can do is increase the wellbeing, those four questions of our employees. And while that doesn’t change the uncertainty of the situation, wellbeing, optimism, having a purpose, being satisfied are good buffers against uncertainty. ADI IGNATIUS: So, are you saying that wellbeing and happiness, there’s a causal effect to business success or that business success leads to wellbeing and happiness? MARTY SELIGMAN: Well, this is what the book Agency is about at length. And that is a question, are these psychological variables like optimism causal or are they determined by the world and the economics? I think the best view is that they’re reciprocally causal. When important developments like the Wright brothers occur, that’s a fact out in the world, heavier than air flight is possible. That in the world causes other people who are working than heavier than air flight to be optimistic that they can now improve on heavier than air flight. They now get into a mental state of agency and they produce better steering. Better steering, the flights now occur for 30 minutes at a time. That increases the optimism of people who are working on long-term effects of heavier than air flight. So, I think the best evidence is not that historical inevitability, material, technological success is the cause, but it causes an increase in agency psychologically and agency causes more trying, more persistence and more innovation, which in turn produces more technological development, which in turn produces more agency. And indeed, I think that’s been the history of the industrial revolution. ADI IGNATIUS: So, if I’m a CEO listening to this conversation and I think, “All right, my organization has become too passive, too risk-averse, has a mindset that nothing we can do is going to turn things around,” what’s the first thing you would tell me to do on Monday morning? MARTY SELIGMAN: The first thing would be let’s measure systematically the optimism and pessimism of your organization. These things are well measured now. Let’s now train the staff, the managers and the people below them with the techniques that decrease pessimism and passivity. So that’s the first Monday morning thing is let’s measure and then counter the pessimism of a company with techniques that are proven to work. ADI IGNATIUS: Marty, thank you very much for being on the HBR IdeaCast. MARTY SELIGMAN: Happy to be here, Adi. ADI IGNATIUS: That was Martin Seligman, professor of psychology at the University of Pennsylvania and author of the new book, Agency: The Psychological History of Human Progress. Check back in the feed on Thursday for the first episode of our series on how AI is fundamentally changing leadership in organizations. In the initial episode, we’ll dive into how it’s affecting talent management and culture. If you found this episode helpful, share it with a colleague and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, please consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter, and unlimited access to HBR online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to senior producer, Mary Dooe and senior production editor, Kristin Murphy Romano, and thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. I’m Adi Ignatius.

item.title: Stop Automating Old Processes. Design New Ones Instead.
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.29
Summary. Companies are pouring money into AI but often failing to generate enterprise-wide returns because they automate individual tasks rather than redesign the workflows that produce business value. Companies are rapidly increasing AI investment, but enterprise returns remain elusive. BCG’s January 2026 “AI Radar,” surveying 640 CEOs across 16 markets, reports that corporations expect to roughly double AI spending this year, from 0.8% of revenue to about 1.7%. Yet PwC’s 2026 “Global CEO Survey” finds that only 12% of CEOs report both revenue and cost benefits, while McKinsey QuantumBlack’s April 2026 analysis finds that 60% of organizations still see no enterprise-wide EBIT impact—even as nearly eight in 10 use generative AI in at least one business function.

item.title: When Persuasion Is (and Isn’t) Manipulation
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.26
Summary. In an interview, Colin Marshall, an ethics professor and author of a new book on persuasion, argues that ethical persuasion begins with treating people as reasoning partners rather than For nearly a century, ambitious professionals have turned to books about persuasion for help getting other people to say yes. From Dale Carnegie’s How to Win Friends and Influence People to more recent work on influence, nudges, and behavioral science, the underlying promise has often been practical: learn how people think, and you can become more effective at moving them. Influence is not only a route to power, but a way of exercising leadership once you have it.

item.title: How GEO Is Changing the Role of Brand Manager
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.04
Share Podcast How GEO Is Changing the Role of Brand Manager As AI increasingly mediates what consumers know, consider, and buy, how does a company’s marketing strategy have to change? AthenaHQ, a startup that helps brands monitor, protect, and optimize their visibility across conversational AI engines like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini was founded in 2025. The company, co-founded by Andrew Yan, built a platform that enables major consumer brands, B2B software companies, and marketing agencies to track their share of voice, correct factual errors in AI responses, and manage their reputation across generative answer engines. In the case, “AthenaHQ: Building Brands for AI Search,” Yan faces a call with a global automaker after its newest vehicle has quietly vanished from chatbot recommendations. He must evaluate the platform’s expansion as he confronts core industry dilemmas: how AI disintermediates traditional marketing, who should own generative engine optimization (GEO) inside an organization, and how to prove value on an unattributable channel. In this episode, Harvard Business School associate professor Julian De Freitas and AthenaHQ co-founder and CEO Andrew Yan join host Brian Kenny to discuss the case, exploring how marketers are navigating the new world of GEO, the so-called “dark funnel” of customer engagement, and the need for brand managers to optimize for brand sentiment and accuracy not just search rankings. BRIAN KENNY: If you want to know what keeps chief marketing officers awake at night, it’s this. For nearly three decades, winning online meant winning the search rankings. Brands learned how to optimize keywords, links, and content so consumers could find them and then decide for themselves what to trust. Generative AI is rewriting those rules. Instead of presenting 10 blue links, AI systems increasingly synthesize information, make comparisons, and offer recommendations of their own. That shift creates a profound challenge for marketers. What happens when an AI confidently tells consumers something about your brand that’s outdated or simply wrong? Today’s case explores the emerging field of generative engine optimization and asks a larger question. When AI increasingly mediates what consumers know, consider, and buy, does the very nature of brand management have to change? Today on Cold Call, we’ll discuss, “AthenaHQ: Building Brands for AI Search,” with case author Julian De Freitas and the company’s co-founder and CEO, Andrew Yan. I’m your host, Brian Kenny, and you’re listening to Cold Call on the HBR Podcast Network. Julian De Freitas’ research addresses questions about how consumers perceive, adopt, and interact with AI systems. Welcome back, Julian. JULIAN DE FREITAS: Always good to be here. BRIAN KENNY: It’s another AI case, just another day for you, right? JULIAN DE FREITAS: Another day in my life, yeah. BRIAN KENNY: Great case. This will be fun. Andrew Yan is the co-founder and CEO of AthenaHQ and the protagonist in today’s case. Welcome, Andrew. ANDREW YAN: Glad to be here. BRIAN KENNY: Welcome to HBS. Following this session you’re going to be heading into an MBA classroom to listen to the students talk about your case and the decisions that you have to make. How are you feeling about that? ANDREW YAN: Yeah, hopefully they have flattering things to say. But the reality of it is as a fast-moving field and being a startup in this field, there are highs and lows. And I think the case covers a lot about what it means to be evolving in this ever-changing field of AI search. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, you’re not joking. It’s changing so fast. And as a person who manages a brand, we are thinking about these things all the time and the impact that AI is having and will continue to have just on the discipline of marketing. It’s hard to know where it’s going. So it’s great that you’re coming here and I think you’ll really enjoy listening to the students and Julian talk about the case. There’s always some great insights that come out there and they’re probably going to learn a ton from listening to you. So why don’t we just dive into our podcast. Julian, I’ll start with you. The case opens with an interesting example. An automaker discovers that a vehicle already on the market is selling well… That’s selling well, rather, is missing from a chatbot’s recommendations because the AI is relying on an old article, an article from 2021. I’m wondering why you decided to choose that moment to open the case and what larger problem does it reveal about brand management and the challenges of that in the age of AI? JULIAN DE FREITAS: Yeah, so I chose this example firstly because it gets your attention. It’s not the sort of mistake a human might typically make, assuming some old article was still relevant. And of course, if you were in charge of that brand, it would be very concerning. But more importantly, I chose that example because it gets at a question that runs throughout the case, which is what’s changing because of AI search? And in particular, is the traditional wisdom around how to build a brand still the same or is it still the same, but maybe the mechanisms have changed? And in this particular example, in some ways it’s the traditional wisdom of have a consistent message, maintain control of authorship of your brand, but the mechanism has changed because the reason you had to be consistent in the past was that consumers have limited memory and they might be confused if they hear multiple things. And here it has more to do with how AI is searching for answers from these different sources to then decide what to feed you. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. How did you hear about AthenaHQ? JULIAN DE FREITAS: I was lucky enough to have this brought to me by Allie in our California case center. Our case centers play such a crucial role in our ability to stay abreast of what’s happening and she connected the dots. She knew what I was interested in and it’s been a perfect marriage since. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, that’s great. We talk about AI search. I can’t tell you how many hours we’ve invested in the marketing community and understanding how to do search engine optimization over the past 10, 15, 20 years. It’s been this thing that everybody’s tried to get better at. And in some ways it feels like that was time wasted. I know it wasn’t and we can talk a little bit about that. But Andrew, let me turn to you for a minute. Can you, thinking about that incident that starts the case, take us inside the conversation with the automaker. And I’m wondering when executives deal with something like this for the first time, what’s their initial reaction? Do they realize they have an AI problem or do they think it’s a bigger brand issue? ANDREW YAN: Yeah, that’s a great point. So with this global automaker, the reaction was, we don’t know what we don’t know. And there are these vestigial structures of our brand, which we didn’t even know were surfaced to AI, that AI is pulling from. And that’s the biggest concern from a brand perspective, from a CMO perspective, from a marketing exec perspective is how do you make sure that you have control over your brand? That’s a big risk. Of course, SEO is about how do you optimize your brand, but with AI, AI has an opinion and that’s a huge difference between SEO and this new space we’re calling generative engine optimization, GEO. Which is AI has an opinion about your brand, it has certain attributes it’ll associate with your brand. Similar to how your best friend, when they recommend your product, they might have opinions about the product. And AI has kind of turned into this sort of best friend recommendation, which knows a lot about you, has opinions about certain brands. And if you’re a brand manager, you care a lot about how is your brand represented on AI. BRIAN KENNY: How did you come up with the idea to start AthenaHQ? ANDREW YAN: Before Athena, I was a product manager on Google search and this was around 2024 when… Before the whole landscape has changed a lot since then. And I remember at Google, I was playing around with the earliest versions of Google AI mode and it would take three to ten seconds for it to get me to a response. And in the traditional search metrics, we’re talking about hundredths of a millisecond latency. And despite this taking three to ten seconds for me to get a response, I found myself gravitating towards using the preview version of AI mode. And that’s when I had this, oh wow moment. This is a different tech that is just objectively a better search experience. And you could kind of draw the line, connect the dots, that latency will improve over time as we all see. Latency has improved so much and it will only get better. And the moment latency drops, we see adoption rise, is a typical trend that we see with search. And we’ve seen that with ChatGPT, with Gemini, with AI Overviews. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. I go back to the days of dial-up modems. So I can tell you we become very patient over time. You had to wait a long time to even get a connection. So Julian, let me come back to you for a minute. The case does a good job drawing the distinction between traditional search and that was the 10 blue bullets that I mentioned. We’re all familiar with getting that long listing of results and then you can pick and choose which one you want. AI takes the different approach, which is to synthesize that information and using some judgment like Andrew was just saying. How does that change the nature of the marketer’s job in that situation? JULIAN DE FREITAS: Yeah, I think it changes it in a couple of ways. One is you need to change your mental model for what you’re doing, what you’re optimizing for. So before, as you mentioned, you’re trying to get ranked in a certain way. Now you’re trying to format content and be present on sources in such a way that this friend, or whatever metaphor that you’re using for the AI engine, wants to include your answer in its own paraphrased answer. So that’s a change in mental model. Relatedly, now that it’s talking conversationally about your brand, there are different metrics that you want to keep track of. So some of them are similar to SEO, like if you’re mentioned and the rank that you’re mentioned, but there are also things like sentiments. So is your brand mentioned in a positive way or negative way? And if it is, how much share do you have of that voice compared to your competitors? And then as our opening example suggests, another factor is, is your brand being represented accurately? So it could be that the AI engine is drawing from a source that’s inaccurately portraying your brand. It could be that it’s hallucinating something about your brand. And so this is a new concern that you have to have on the top of your mind because of how that interface is changing. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. Andrew, what’s the value proposition that AthenaHQ offers to clients when you’re trying to convince them that this is an important thing for them to pay attention to? ANDREW YAN: To put it shortly, we help brands see, act, and win on AI search. And there’s a monitoring part of how do you, like Julian mentioned, how do you see where your gaps are, where your weaknesses are? Being able to pinpoint with very pinpoint accuracy where those are coming from. Is it coming from this page on your website? Is it coming from your social pages? Is it coming from a third-party page? And then acting is the critical part and that’s where Athena specializes in, is how do we help marketing teams market faster? And it’s about marketing velocity as well where different verticals are starting to move much faster than before with fast- moving consumer goods, for example, or software. These spaces are moving really fast. And this is an adjacent challenge we’re also tackling is when you’re marketing to AI, AI can change its opinion on a dime and you need to be able to change your marketing engine, so to speak as well and be agile. So that’s a whole other component that we work on. BRIAN KENNY: The opening example is a really interesting one where it’s drawing on an article that’s old, five, six, seven years old. The information’s not up to date. We know that AI hallucinates. We know there’s the potential for it to provide information that’s not completely accurate or it puts an inflection on it that’s just not quite right. How do you combat something like that? ANDREW YAN: Yeah, on multiple levels. So how we address this is we have a brand hub, we call it Knowledge Base, where we collect thousands of facts about your brand. And we’re able to cross reference that against the set of AI responses and see when AI responses contradict each other or contradict your brand hub. And from there we will detect where AI is hallucinating, where it’s deviating from your brand. And this really scales up, especially if you’re a multinational brand, you have such a scale of facts you need to manage as a brand that a human can’t do that. And it used to be in the past that you’d have a human probably in the legal department who would have a checklist of these are all the approved facts that we can have out. And to some degree that’s still true, but how do we augment that with AI to make sure that brand management is possible at a global scale? BRIAN KENNY: Okay. We’re coming from a place where there was sort of one dominant algorithm that was Google that all the searches were derived from there. And now you’re getting into a situation where you’ve got multiple different AI platforms. I’m wondering how do we think about the brand managing its reputation when you have to be able to be managing multiple different sources of information? JULIAN DE FREITAS: Yeah, it’s true. And I mean, the case talks about the distribution of sources, for instance, that the different models are pulling from where some like Copilot might pull from seven sources and then you have Grok that’s pulling from 20 something sources. And so there’s such a fragmented landscape. I think one concern brands should have is that they may be positioned differently across these models. There have been some preliminary studies showing that 55% of the time you might be positioned differently on one platform versus another. So being aware of that and is your brand consistently portrayed is one factor. But I think also knowing who your target market is. So for example, if you’re selling an enterprise software solution, you probably want to prioritize Copilot because that’s where your customer might see you. And if you’re a consumer brand, let’s say that’s going to be less relevant. Another factor would be just coverage. So if you don’t have a strong opinion on which particular model you need to be on, you might just track where is most of the search volume happening. Most of it still is on Google because that’s where the AI Overviews lie. And then we have ChatGPT and you can track it from there. And then I also think of this in terms of diversification. So you don’t want to put all your eggs in just one model or even certain sources that you know a model likes because as Andrew alluded to, this is a shifting landscape. So you don’t want to lose sight of the bigger picture, which is have a consistent picture of your brand, be on enough of these models because at the end of the day, these AI models are trying to corroborate truths about you. And so that’s what you need to sort of keep your attention on. BRIAN KENNY: And I would assume they want to be right. I mean, can we assume that the AI wants to get it right? Is that a safe assumption? JULIAN DE FREITAS: I would say they want to be aligned with what humans would want and enjoy. And especially for certain technical questions, it’s going to want to be right. And then there are going to be other questions like what are the best trousers that it’s going to want to give you a useful picture that’s related to you in a personalized way. BRIAN KENNY: Okay. ANDREW YAN: And I can add to this too. Fundamentally, AI is looking for the shortest path to an answer. And whether that shortest path goes through your own content or if it goes through earned content, it doesn’t really care. And that’s the scary part from a brand management perspective. BRIAN KENNY: It seems a little exhausting as a brand, again, I’ll speak as a brand manager to be able to manage all these different things. We’re talking about citations, share of voice sentiment, factual accuracy. As you’re thinking about giving guidance to your clients and to marketing leaders, what do you tell them to pay attention to? Is there something they should pay attention to more than something else? ANDREW YAN: Yeah. So my overall philosophy is to simplify the field of AI search for our customers. What that means is that there are thousands of potential dimensions you could be looking at the data from, but from a marketing leadership perspective, we help simplify based on here are the axes that truly matter for your brand. Here’s a blueprint across, as Julian referenced, the AI models that matter the most for your brand, depending on your vertical and who you’re targeting and who your personas are. And based on that, we provide a customized blueprint for each brand. So it’s not a general landscape, here’s what it looks like for all brands, but if you’re a semiconductor company, here’s a plan specifically for your semiconductor audience. If you’re an automobile manufacturer, here’s a plan specifically for your audience and it expands. BRIAN KENNY: Okay. So that’s kind of what you were referring to before. It’s got to be depending on who your customer base is, what your sector is, things are going to be a little bit different for you. Can you describe, because the case refers to the dark funnel, that sounds very mysterious. Can you describe what that is? JULIAN DE FREITAS: Yeah. So I mean, first of all, for those in the audience who are not familiar with the marketing funnel, that’s the whole customer journey from being aware of your brand to eventually considering and comparing options and evaluating which one you’re going to choose and then having the intent to buy, and ultimately buying. And there’ve always been some parts of that journey that have been dark just because we don’t own every touchpoint that a customer might have as they’re researching the brand. So maybe we own the social page and our own branded website, but we don’t own some review site. So what’s fascinating about AI engines is that more of the funnel is becoming dark. And Andrew’s research and some other research I’ve seen suggests that that darkening is happening especially at the discovery phase at the top of the funnel and at the consideration and evaluation phase in the middle of the funnel. So if you think about it, that funnel is both collapsing into one touch point with the AI engine where you’re discovering and researching and comparing and evaluating, and all of that is not owned. So there’s a darkening that’s happening. And one of the symptoms that the case describes that this might be happening to you is that you’re seeing less referral traffic from touch points like an ad you put out, let’s say. BRIAN KENNY: 100%, yeah. JULIAN DE FREITAS: You’re seeing more direct traffic and then they’re staying in that session shorter with you before they buy. And so it suggests that they’ve already done the research elsewhere, probably on an AI engine, and then they’re coming to you. BRIAN KENNY: But the fear that, I’ll speak for my marketing brethren here, the fear that a lot of us have is that people aren’t clicking through to your content. They’re looking at the AI search results. It’s nicely synthesized for them. They can get all the information they need there and they’re not necessarily clicking all the way through into your web presence. So I mean, how do you think about advising somebody on how to deal with that kind of a situation, Andrew? ANDREW YAN: It’s a sign of the times, right? BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. ANDREW YAN: The shift to AI platforms in terms of search behavior is just as big of a shift as a shift from web to mobile, almost more than a decade ago. And we’re only going to see this trend continue. In terms of specific vertical KPIs and how that impacts, for example, in the field of e-commerce, we’ve seen that average order value for carts where the shopper is coming from AI is sometimes double or more than traditional traffic. They’re converting at higher rates across the board, across multiple industries that we’re seeing. And also they’re staying sometimes shorter, but sometimes longer on certain pages, specifically on these checkout pages, where it’s clear that the buyers have done the research elsewhere, probably on AI and they’re coming back just to check out. BRIAN KENNY: Okay. So that’s the dark funnel. We don’t know where it’s happening, but somewhere in there the buyer’s making an informed decision about what they want to do. Andrew, I’m wondering how often you encounter a situation where someone’s digital presence, whether it’s their website or other sources of information, is conflicting in and of itself, right? We all like to think that the information that’s on our websites is accurate and up to date, but does this journey begin with me taking a look across the thousands and thousands of pages that Harvard Business School has on its website? ANDREW YAN: So we do a lot of that for you. If you were to go through each one- BRIAN KENNY: This is like a therapy session for me. This is great. ANDREW YAN: Yeah. Maybe that’s my second career as a therapist, right? No, we build this brand profile automatically and it compounds through time. I can tell you a story about how other brands have managed this in the real world. So a very large financial institution used by, I believe millions of Americans, we found that one of their pricing pages about their mortgage rates was off, and it was using the old rate from a few years ago. BRIAN KENNY: Ooh, that’s a biggie. ANDREW YAN: It’s huge, right? BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. ANDREW YAN: Financial institutions have been fined millions of dollars for this problem. And that’s an example of you don’t know what you don’t know. This dark funnel is really very dark for a lot of CMOs. And in this analogy, we help turn on the lights, or we provide a flashlight where we’re not going to be able to see everything, but the flashlight, depending on where you point it, we’re able to focus on certain parts of the business that matter the most. BRIAN KENNY: Julian, I want to talk about Reddit for a minute because the case points out, and I actually heard recently, as recent as this morning, I think when I was telling somebody about the conversation we were going to be having, that Reddit calls itself the largest LLM in media. Which might be true, but in my experience jumping around Reddit, it’s not all very helpful information. It seems like there’s a lot of noise. So I’m wondering how Reddit factors into this equation because it seems like it factors in pretty strongly. JULIAN DE FREITAS: Yeah. The case describes that one of the most popular sources that these models draw from is Reddit, also YouTube, LinkedIn. And then you go down the list and then you start to see the usual culprits that we would typically think of as being authoritative, like Forbes. I think it says a few things. So one, at least historically, a site like Reddit is a place that you can crawl. And at the end of the day, again, these AI engines want to corroborate any answers. And so you can get some corroboration from a source like this. As you point out, it’s not all technical stuff on Reddit, but I think that’s also okay because in many cases, the types of questions are, what is the best this or what should I use for that? And so in those sort of cases, you want a chorus of opinions, rather than just one authoritative voice, even if it is very authoritative. I think if there are cases where the user is asking a very technical question, then you should expect that technical sources will be used for that, but that’s not happening all the time. But I think the scary part is that maybe ordinarily speaking, before AI search, you wouldn’t have gone on Reddit or YouTube, let’s say, as part of your customer journey. And now they’re actually influencing what you come away with in terms of what to do. And again, that’s a non-owned site. So it’s a different world that we are living in. BRIAN KENNY: Right. No doubt. So let me ask you, Andrew, once you discover what’s truly influencing AI as it relates to your brand, is there an intervention you can do? Or is intervening going to cause more problems than it solves? ANDREW YAN: I would say there are three types of interventions, broadly speaking, and that’s precisely where we specialize in. First is how do you, I call this vestigial content. How do you manage vestigial content, which you didn’t know was out there? Like in the example in the case, these content pieces which are providing outdated information or false information, that’s no longer true. We see this a lot with pricing specifications, and also if you’re a brand which has acquired multiple other brands and you’re conglomerating this house of brands, how do you manage that? So that’s the first type. Second type is optimizing existing content. Third is how do you figure out what types of net new content to be putting out to be optimizing for the AI engines? I like to use this term, the surface area of search, because managing a brand today on AI means that you have to manage a much broader surface area of search, which Athena centralizes. And we built Athena to centralize across multiple different channels, across social, PR, on page, all of these. In the old world, you have 10 blue links, majority of people would only click on the first three, and you’d only care really about the first three. Once you got to the first three, job done, we’re good here. Now off the shelf AI can pull from 20, 30, 40, and not to mention deep research can pull from hundreds. So as you see AI move more towards deep-research style of reasoning and analysis, the surface area just keeps on growing. The other nuance here is that not every source is weighed equally. Some sources are weighed more than others. So how do you piece together the interventions in the most quantitative way where you get the biggest bang for your buck? Because you don’t want to be doing a lot of actions without much payoff. If you’re doing a lot of actions, but they’re not the most impactful, then you’re just running around. BRIAN KENNY: And this is another sort of additive thing. It seems like every time a new marketing technology or platform or approach comes along, it doesn’t replace the thing before it. It adds to the thing before it. So we’re piling on more and more things on top of each other. And here, one of the things the case points out is that marketers might need to be thinking about optimizing both for humans and how humans think about and ask questions, and also machines and what the machine is looking for and how it’s responding to those questions. Can you talk a little bit about that challenge for marketers? JULIAN DE FREITAS: Yeah, it’s a challenge in the first place because humans and machines perceive the world in very different ways. Humans are very visual, we’re compelled by imagery and videos, and there’s experiential brands and emotional brands that move us. And then you have something like these AI engines, which, if they’re looking at a video, they’re actually taking screenshots of it and then reasoning over the frames. It’s not that they’re experiencing something when they watch the video. And if they say that the video is beautiful, it might be because someone said that and they’re sort of repeating that. And I think the sort of tension is that let’s say you’re one of these brands that has historically invested in this kind of imagery. Now at the same time, you need to provide content that’s going to be easy for AI to digest because it’s not going to spend a lot of time on your website before it gives up. So that could mean FAQs, it could mean tables of comparisons and that sort of thing. And so the tension is if you’re catering too much toward one side or the other, are you hurting the experience, let’s say for people who previously really enjoyed the imagery and all of that that you’re putting on your website. So I like to think of this as a spectrum. In the middle, you’re trying to do both. On the one end, you’re saying, “I’m not going to change anything for AI. I hope that it’s just going to catch up and figure out how to parse my human readable website.” And then on the other end of the spectrum, I’m just going to have two different websites. BRIAN KENNY: Oh, that’s interesting. Yeah, like a shadow website. JULIAN DE FREITAS: Exactly, like a shadow website. And the case goes into why that may or may not be a good idea. BRIAN KENNY: It seems like a terrible idea to me, to be honest with you. One is enough, and then having another website to manage would be super challenging. Julian and I had a conversation, I don’t know, I think it was last spring or so with a firm. He wrote a case about a firm called BrandBastion that manages automated replies to customers who are writing in to comment or ask questions to. I’m not doing it justice. But the question here has to do with automation and how much should we automate with regard to AI and how we think about the brand? And how much should we stay involved because judgment matters? And how do you differentiate between the two? We’ve been talking a lot at Harvard Business School about the fact that we want our students to embrace AI. We’re trying to find ways to bring it into the curriculum through cases and through assignments and through the research that our faculty do. At the same time, we believe deeply that human judgment will be the sort of mark of distinction between leaders who know how to navigate through these kinds of technologies and lead through them. And automation is great, but only to a certain extent. So long-winded way of saying how much should stay automated? How much of it should really stay in the hands of humans? ANDREW YAN: That’s a great question. I’ve always been very humans-first approach. How I think about it is the way we’re doing marketing, both for our customers, but also at Athena is: AI is kind of the back office and humans are the front office and let humans do what humans do best, like conversations or exchanging ideas with other humans. There’s a lot of rote repetitive work in marketing and many other disciplines in general as well, which a human shouldn’t be doing that work. For example, when you’re optimizing your content, one aspect is how do you format the content? Our philosophy is no human should ever have to think about that. You should be thinking more about the messaging than about how am I going to format this? And we just bake that into our process. So using Athena, our customers don’t even have to think about formatting. We do the formatting for them, push it to the CMS, the content management system. It all happens without them thinking about it. And then they can focus more on the positioning, the messaging, this more strategic part, which is so much more valuable. BRIAN KENNY: Julian, I’m wondering as you think about this, in the broader landscape, do we need to completely retool our organizations? Do we need to change the way that we’re thinking about roles within the marketing organization to address this? Or is this just a slighter shift where we have to maybe change our way of thinking versus the actual roles? JULIAN DE FREITAS: I don’t think I would go out and recommend that everybody hire a head of GEO. In part because when you hire for a role, then part of what you’re communicating is, oh, this is a specialized function and it’s no one else’s responsibility. Whereas we’ve just been talking about how this combines SEO and social and optimizing your own content. So really, I think whoever in the organization is typically responsible for coordinating these various functions should be activated to lead this and get people looking at the same dashboard. So I don’t think a dramatic reorg is necessary, but these different functions do need to find a way to work together so that they’re facing the same north star. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. Okay. That’s great. So our time is almost up. This has been a great conversation as I knew it would be. I’ve got one question left for each of you and I’ll end with Julian since he wrote the case. So let me start with you, Andrew. If you were to look down the road, say five years and you’re advising that same client that was featured in the beginning of the case about what’s happening, what do you think the landscape would look like? That’s a little far into the future for AI, I know, but just thinking forward, what do you think brand marketers are going to need to be able to adapt to continue to thrive in this era? ANDREW YAN: I think a lot about this concept of semi-autonomous marketing. Which is we’re based in San Francisco, I ride more self-driving cars now than I ride human driven cars. And in autonomous cars it’s a concept of autonomy, levels of autonomy. And it feels like we’re still at one autonomy with most marketing orgs that we work with. I think where we’ll end up three, four, five years from now is where humans are in the loop, but in the highest leveraged positions in the loop. And even with large clients where there’s more structure, more of a marketing force behind it, I think we’re going to see humans being this upper part of the org chart.
